Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Are there any telescopes pointed towards Earth from outer space? If not, why?
Answer: There are lots of them. Some are weather satellites. One which is particularly fun is this: Yep, real-time full-disk Earth pictures from space. There are a lot of satellites that capture specific images on demand as well, used for things like Google Earth and geoscience, plus military purposes.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is assembly faster than C? If yes, why is it not used more often for performance critical applications in embedded or high-performance computing?
Answer: Assembly is marginally faster than C if given enough attention to optimisation, but it’s quite a bit of work to match C’s performance. Assembly is also many times slower than C to write, maybe 10x slower. And the bigger the program, the slower it gets to write. So, sensible people don’t write assembly unless they absolutely have to, and even then try to minimise how much they use. C has another massive advantage: if you might need to run on another processor (and you probably will one day), that’s actually possible and usually easy. Assembler you have to start from scratch again. If your CPU has this one feature you absolutely have to use… write an inline assembler wrapper for it so you can call it from C, or add an intrisic to your compiler.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the purpose of the small plug by the gear change lever on automatic transmission cars?
Answer: That gives access to unlock the shifter if the car won’t start and you need to put it in neutral to tow it, or for various operations you might need to do during a repair.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How can I figure how much assembly language I will need to use to make a game where every millisecond is crucial to ensure good response and max performance well using C++ for the majority of the codebase?
Answer: Easy: Zero. These days, there are three or four places you need assembler: if you’re working on code for a really tiny chip (if the whole computer costs a few cents), if you’re working on a compiler, or if you’re working on an operating system kernel. And, just maybe, if you’re working on a fundamental library. Otherwise, just forget it. Compilers are good enough, and you’re probably going to have to deal with GPUs anyway. For a modern computer, even if it’s a phone, a millisecond is an eternity. Even a microsecond is a pretty long time. You can do a system call and get an answer in under 20 nanoseconds, from C++, if the kernel has the answer handy.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to write a compiler using any programming language, or does it have to be written in assembly or low-level languages like C or C++?
Answer: It’s possible in almost any language. Production compilers for many languages are written in C++ because there are good libraries for doing so. But many compilers are written in the language they compile, too, so they can compile themselves (how that is possible is too long for this answer; the short version is you have to start with a compiler for at least a subset of the language that is written in something else). Some languages are not very suitable for writing a compiler, so while it would be possible it’s unlikely you would do it. You do not have to write a compiler in assembly, and should not. It hasn’t been necessary for a very long time. Small snippets of assembly, though, are often found in compilers. They’re there to become part of the target programs; you have to teach the compiler what the assembly or machine code of the target looks like. One way is to supply assembly code, another is to supply blocks of machine code, and the common way for newer compilers is to use an intermediate language which is kind of an abstract assembly language for no particular processor, which is then given to a specialised library to translate to the real machine code.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: I've an idea to design all my programs to work within 4GB of RAM and 1GHz x86-64 processors. Is C good enough for most of the program with Assembly language for the most critical tasks?
Answer: Any modern language will work fine for most jobs on that class of machine. You probably don’t need to touch assembly at all, unless you’re writing an OS kernel, and even then there might only need to be a couple of hundred lines in the whole OS. Honestly, it sounds like you’re a bit out of your depth here. Which language am I going to do everything in is a beginner question… choose languages for the good of each project. They’re not hard to learn.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it true that smartphones today are more powerful than the Cray-2 supercomputers?
Answer: Yes, it is. An iPhone 14 Pro has about 10% higher vector floating point performance than a Cray 2. That’s what the Cray was optimised for, the iPhone has an even bigger advantage for other kinds of performance. A high-end modern desktop has an enormous advantage over the Cray, could easly be 10x. Modern supercomputers are on entirely another planet, being tens of thousands of times faster again.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to replace all propeller-driven aircraft with modern turbofan-powered alternatives without sacrificing speed and range, given enough money and resources?
Answer: No, it isn’t. Jets are not always better, and the reason we still use propellers is that they do jobs that you can’t do with a jet, or they’re cheaper to run in their role. Jets cruise slightly faster and higher than turboprops, using less fuel in the cruise. But turboprops accelerate, climb, decelerate and descend faster, and use less fuel in takeoff and climb. Turboprops can also use substantially shorter runways. That means turboprops can use airports a jet just can’t, and even if a jet could do the flight, if it’s a short flight the turboprop may well be cheaper and even possibly faster. Jets and turboprops both get much less efficient as they get smaller. So for the smallest airplanes, there is no sense in using them as the fuel economy will be terrible. Instead, you use gasoline or diesel piston engines with propellers. When we have a suitable battery technology, electric aircraft will be using propellers to start with, it will take quite some time before ducted fans (the electric equivalent of jets) start making sense.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for supercomputers to become significantly smaller and more powerful in the future?
Answer: By definition, supercomputers are the fastest reasearch computers of their time. So, as technology progresses, supercomputers are upgraded or replaced by new machines using the latest tech. Therefore, while you might eventually be able to get a desktop, or eventually even laptop, that outperforms a current supercomputer… by the time you can, a supercomputer will still be tens of thousands of times faster. After all… if you have a research problem that big, you fill a warehouse with current generation servers, and there’s your supercomputer. Ok, it’s a little more complicated than that, but the essence remains: if you can afford the hardware, using a ton of space and power lets you do bigger computations.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What causes the wings to stall before the tail of an airplane?
Answer: Deliberate design. Planes are designed so that the horizontal tail will stall at an angle of attack greater than that required to stall the wing. Usually that’s only for an upright stall, though for aerobatic aircraft and fighters they typically require this for inverted stalls as well. Why? Turns out it’s hard to recognise that you’ve stalled the tail, and relatively easy to recognise that the wing is stalled. So it’s safer. Also, some takeoff and landing techniques are more useful if you can easily and reliably fully stall the wing during the process.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: I want a definitive answer according to science.. Did the universe exist before the Big Bang or not?
Answer: Science does not have a definitive answer to that question. Sorry. Our current model of the universe starts more or less working a tiny fraction of a second after the Big Bang. Before that, it produces no reasonable results. That means the model is incomplete, for sure, but there’s presently no evidence on which to base extending the model back further. So, until we have that evidence and the resulting theories… we can’t say anything useful. Our current model also implies that “before the Big Bang” is not a time that could exist. But since that’s inside the area where the theory is incomplete, you shouldn’t take that as being definitive.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Modern passenger jets are very powerful, but if you stood one up on its end like a rocket and gave it full throttle, would it get off the ground?
Answer: No. Not even close. Some jet fighters would. But a commercial airplane has no need for that much thrust, and jet fighters pay for it in absurd fuel consumption.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can someone get hired by companies like Google or Facebook without advanced knowledge in computer science and programming?
Answer: Sure. But you have to have advanced knowledge in something the company is interested in. Sales, finance, some kinds of law. Data centers employ quite a lot of industrial electricians and HVAC technicians. Or lots of experience as a manager in tech.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Are there any electric cars that can match the speed and acceleration of internal combustion engine cars? If not, is there a projected timeline for when electric cars may catch up in terms of speed and acceleration?
Answer: Electric cars hold the production car lap records on many famous race tracks. So, when are the combustion cars going to catch up? Probably never.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can a person with no knowledge of electrical engineering or technology build their own electric car with full autonomy, similar to Teslas?
Answer: I’m going with “no”. Not because the individual pieces of that project are impossible to learn; they’re not. It’s because you won’t live long enough to finish. There are projects that are just far too big for an individual, and this is definitely one of those. Remove the “full autonomy” bit, yeah, sure, you could learn enough to do that. EVs aren’t all that complicated. But self-driving is very, very hard, and there are no off-the-shelf solutions. It is remotely possible that there may be off the shelf solutions within 20 years or so, we shall see. But as it stands right now, that part is just not doable. Also… self-driving off-road or in a controlled environment? Still no off the shelf solutions, but it’s a whole lot easier than on public roads. So if you limit it that way… just barely possible, maybe. Race tracks or the inside of a warehouse, possibly. You’re still up for the equivalent of an electrical engineering degree with a speciality in control systems as just part of the set-up for that project.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to drive an electric vehicle with the engine off using only the battery?
Answer: What engine? A true EV doesn’t even have an engine. Only batteries and electric motors.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What makes electric vehicles (EVs) heavy? Is it possible to create lighter EVs with similar range and performance as the Tesla Model S?
Answer: EV batteries are really heavy. So far as we know, there’s nothing implausible about much lighter batteries. We just don’t know how to make them. It’s therefore quite plausible that we will see much lighter EVs with better range. Performance doesn’t really need to improve, it’s already a bit silly.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why does a plane drop suddenly when it encounters an air pocket?
Answer: There’s not really such a thing as an “air pocket”. But yes, planes do occasionally drop suddenly. They don’t drop very far, our senses greatly exaggerate the sense of falling. It’s just wind. Near the ground, the wind is always nearly parallel to the ground. But at altitude, the wind can blow in any direction (inside a thunderstorm cell, for example, there are very strong vertical winds blowing straight up). If you fly into some descending air, the plane turns a slight downward corner, which you experience as a sudden drop. Remember, planes fly very, very fast, so you can get a real bump. If you fly small planes, on a windy day you can easily find places where the wind will be changing vertical direction and play with this; above every hill there will be some turbulence and some vertical motion. Sometimes you can find rising air strong enough that you can fly the plane without the engine. Glider pilots become experts in exploiting the movement of the air, and can fly for as long as they like without an engine, given suitable weather. Obviously they’re looking for rising air rather than descending.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can pilots detect a downward spiral or stall before seeing the altimeter needle move?
Answer: Stall or spin: yes, because the altimeter isn’t going to tell you anything interesting anyway. A plane can stall in any attitude and with any vertical speed; some aerobatic moves require stalling the plane out of a vertical climb. You detect stalls by the position of the controls, and by an angle of attack instrument if you have one. The stalls out of level flight you do in training often begin with a little climb. Spiral dive: not necessarily. This is a 1g situation, the airplane is not stalled, and the pilot’s senses don’t report anything useful. So, if the instruments say the plane is turning, accelerating and descending, it’s in a spiral dive whatever the pilot’s senses tell them is happening. This is why instrument flying is hard; without visual reference, your senses can lose lock on the actual situation, and start lying. The plane’s instruments can too, but you can cross-check between those to determine the real situation.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the carry-on baggage policy for airplanes? Can passengers bring two bags on board? How are they counted (by weight or size)?
Answer: It’s all in the conditions for your ticket, which means mostly it varies by airline. One constant is that there is a maximum weight limit for cabin baggage, which is set by the regulator in the country where the plane is registered. It’s usually about 7 kg, but varies a bit. Otherwise… check the airline rules.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Are there any other possible numbers of cylinders for an internal combustion engine besides 4, 6, and 8?
Answer: Of course. Engines have been made with every number of cylinders from 1 to 18, and also multiples of 6, 8, 9 and 11 above that. Many of those numbers are of course very rare, or only used in specific kinds of engines.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for pilots to recover from spins? Is practicing spin recovery part of their flight training or just a theoretical concept taught in the curriculum?
Answer: Some airplanes can recover from spins, some can not. Some are almost impossible to spin in the first place. Pilots can recover any recoverable airplane, and the recovery procedure is part of the type rating. In some cases the recovery procedure is as simple as “release the controls, throttle back, and wait”. Or it may require placing the controls in a specific position (centered and all the way forward is common). However, not every country requires actual spin training as part of the license process. Many common training airplanes are in the “almost impossible to spin” category. Nearly all large airplanes are in the “can not recover” category. So flying schools would most likely have to specifically buy an aerobatic airplane for the purpose of spin training, which is rather onerous. Training always does cover incipient spins and how to recognise that the next thing that happens would be a spin, and how to recover before the spin becomes fully developed. Nearly all airplanes can recover from an incipient spin, and the exceptions are all very unusual military types.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it easier for musicians to learn a new instrument compared to non-musicians? What factors contribute to this?
Answer: Yes, it’s easier to learn your second and later instruments. That’s because when you start out in music you have a lot to learn about music, how it works, how to keep time, and so on. That comes under the headings of “ear training”, “rhythm training” and “music theory”. All of that stuff is the same for all instruments, but you have to learn it alongside your first. Go to learn a second instrument and you can skip all that because you already know it. Also, there are similarities between some instruments that you can leverage. For example, there’s certain things that all or most stringed instruments have in common.

Question: What happens if we cover half of the lens horizontally?
Answer: This sounds like a great question to answer by experiment. Try it and see. Obviously try not to get anything sticky on the optics when you do, but otherwise it’s harmless. What it actually does will depend rather a lot on the particular lens.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What are the barriers preventing all cars from being fully electric in the near future? Is the current practice of converting non-electric cars into hybrid/electric versions hindering progress towards this goal?
Answer: There’s no barrier, other than that pesky word ‘near’ in the question. It will take quite some time, and it will likely never be absolutely all cars. It would be OK if there were some other non-GHG solutions in the mix too, of course, though it’s unlikely hydrogen will be one of those no matter how much various financial interests would like that. But… people don’t just throw out working machines unless there’s a compelling reason. So we have to wait for them to age out and become unmaintainable, or until the fuel becomes hard to get and too inconvenient. So… for values of ‘near’ like “within 20 years or so”… yeah, it’ll be almost impossible to buy a new combustion car.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can a plane be designed with straight horizontal wings without significantly decreasing its efficiency?
Answer: Yes, it can. The slight angle between the wings of most planes and the horizontal is not about efficiency, it’s about controllability. That angle makes the plane want to fly level, which produces much nicer handling and better safety. Straight horizontal wings and no tail at all would be close to the most efficient airplane possible… but it would be very hard to give it acceptable handling, and it would be even harder to make it safe. Hard is not impossible, however: The military, of course, has rather different standards for acceptable handling and safety than a civilian regulator.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a reason why airplanes only have two wings instead of four? Would having four wings make them more stable and safer during take-off and landing?
Answer: Four wings doesn’t really change the stability or safety of an airplane either way. However, it’s a fact of life in aerodynamics that every corner between a lifting surface and something else, including the tips of the wings, creates more drag, and therefore costs fuel. If you have four wings, you have four wing tips instead of two, and maybe some more corners where the extra wings connect with the fuselage as well. Since more than half of an airplane’s drag comes from the wing tips… you just added at least 50% to the fuel bill. Probably more, since you’d likely make the second wing shorter, and that reduces the efficiency of the wing too. So while this looks cool: With roughly the same technology, you can build this: And the second plane will have a much longer range and better fuel consumption, using an identical engine and at the same weight. (Note: I don’t know that the two pictured airplanes are that close in design, though they very well could be) But remember what I said about corners? Well, that’s why a modern airliner looks like this: Nothing sticking out that doesn’t absolutely need to be, the absolute minimum of corners anywhere, and the winglets actually help with the wing tips quite a lot. It is actually possible to do away with wing tips, though the resulting airplane looks really silly: Yes, that’s real, and it does fly. Zero corners between the wing and anything else.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Has there been a recorded instance of a successful airplane landing with only one functional wing due to in-flight damage?
Answer: Yes, it has been done several times. At least twice that I can recall well enough to recount. Once with an F15 after a mid-air collision. The crew of the other aircraft ejected successfully. The F15 has a very wide fuselage, so provided there’s enough runway this is apparently not even that difficult. Once with a Zlin aerobatic plane after one of its wing retaining bolts broke, such that the wing was attached but would fold up. The pilot solved this one by flying back to the airfield upside down, then making his approach knife-edge (in otherwords, using power and fuselage lift to stay airborne), and only rolling upright at the last second. The plane was even repairable. There are other real occurences. The common factor is that the airplanes are either highly aerobatic, or combat aircraft. It requires a very tough airframe and a lot of power for this to be survivable. It happens quite frequently with model airplanes, too. I’ve seen this done myself, actually. But, so far as I know all the videos you will find online are either completely fake, or video of an incident with a model that is being presented as a full size airplane.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What happens if one wing of a plane is higher than the other?
Answer: It turns away from the higher wing. This is actually how you turn a plane normally, roll it slightly in the direction you want to go (and give other control inputs to stay level and balanced). Most planes, if you do nothing, will tend to tighten the turn by lifting the high wing, leading to a situation called a ‘spiral dive’. It’s easy to fix though… just roll the wings back level.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the difference between the flight mechanisms of helicopters and airplanes? Why do helicopters need their rotors moving to fly, while airplanes can stay on the ground with their motors running?
Answer: Helicopters can stay on the ground with their engines running too, with the rotors at full speed. Both airplanes and helicopters use lift from airfoil surfaces moving fast through the air. For a plane, that’s the wings, for a helicopter it’s the rotor blades. The fundamental difference is this: airplanes create lift by moving the whole airplane through the air, while helicopters create lift by moving only the rotor blades. Essentially, a helicopter flies its wings in circles around the aircraft. This allows a helicopter to fly in any direction, or to hover. It seriously complicates controlling a helicopter, though. Part of that is having control over the rotor blade pitch, both the average pitch during a rotation (called collective pitch) and the change in pitch as the blades move (called cyclic pitch). This allows a helicopter to move the center of lift of the rotor disc around relative to the center of mass, as well as change the total amount of lift. Set the collective to zero on the ground, you make no lift, and the machine won’t fly. Adjust the collective and you can make more or less lift as required. Move the cyclic and the difference between the center of lift and the center of mass will cause the machine to start rotating in the direction you moved the cyclic (the control linkages that make this work are mind-bending, but that’s the effect). Most helicopters also have a tail rotor with pitch control also; that’s to prevent the torque of the engine spinning the machine around, and provide directional control. Even without a tail rotor, there has to be some system to counter torque. One way is to use two or more rotors, there are others. The aerodynamics of helicopters are very complicated, so this didn’t even scratch the surface, but I hope I did show the basic principle.
