Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Does entering Russian territory for tourism and having a Russian stamp in my passport affect my chances of obtaining a visa for the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, United Kingdom, Ireland, and the Schengen Area?
Answer: I don’t think it would, in those particular cases. However, if that’s a concern… most countries allow you to request an additional passport for precisely this reason. There are countries that will never issue a visa if they find an entry stamp from certain other countries… but you don’t have to use the same passport for every country.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What happens to your old passport after it's been replaced by a new one? Can someone else use it before it expires?
Answer: Only you can use your passport, legally. However, it is possible to have two valid passports at the same time. Sometimes you have to present your old one when collecting the new passport, and the old one will be marked invalid (for example, by cutting a corner off the photo page, and usually the cover as well). Other times the issuing authority will just let the old one expire, and for a time you’ll have two. Sometimes people have to travel to countries that have a long visa process and require you to give them the passport you will be using (e.g. Russia), which obviously means you can’t travel elsewhere while they have it, sometimes people need to travel to two countries that will hassle you if you have a visa or entry stamp from each other (Jordan and Israel), and many governments will allow you to request a second passport so you can avoid these problems.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What happens if someone loses their passport before a flight and cannot obtain a new one in time? Will they still be allowed to board the airplane?
Answer: They will not be allowed to check in or pass security. If you lose it in the airport, you might get on the plane, but you’ll be in serious difficulty when you get off, so it’s a better idea to tell the airline what happened and stay where you are.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it legal to fly a small plane without a license if your parents own it?
Answer: Not unless you have someone with an instructor rating and a license in the other pilot seat (which means no single seat planes). You also need the owner’s permission, of course, and there will be some insurance issues as well so it may not be all that cheap.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can someone fly an airplane without a pilot's license, only as a passenger?
Answer: If you fly with someone who has an instructor rating on their license, yes. They’re the pilot-in-command for legal purposes, but they’re allowed to let you handle the controls.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for a commercial airplane to fly with only one engine? How often does this occur?
Answer: Single engine airplanes can be used for some commercial operations, so for those aircraft it is routine. However, I suspect you mean “Can a twin-engine airliner fly on one engine?” To which the answer is… yes, but no pilot will start a flight with only one working engine. Nevertheless, if one fails, even during takeoff with no room to stop, the airplane will fly well enough to make it back to a safe landing. Flights are planned such that there’s no time the airplane is too far from somewhere to land in case of an engine failure. With one engine failed, the airplane will be slower, use more fuel, and will have to fly lower, so it may not be possible to complete the flight to the original destination. There’s always a plan, though. As for how often it occurs… it’s very rare in commercial service. Most pilots go a whole career without having a for-real engine failure in a large airplane.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the reason for planets moving in elliptical orbits instead of circular ones? Is it physically impossible for them to have perfectly circular orbits?
Answer: It’s not physically impossible for an orbit to be circular for a while, but it is absurdly improbable. There is only one circular orbit with a given amount of orbital energy, while there is an infinite family of elliptical orbits with the same energy. Circular orbits are also unstable, in the sense that peturbations from the other objects in the Solar System will cause the orbit to deviate from circularity (and even the galaxy’s tides would do it over a long enough period). Given all that, it’s actually a little surprising that most of the planets have orbits that are as close as they are to circular. The reason for that has to do with orbital resonances, which mean that there is a tendency for the elliptical orbits to become somewhat less elliptical over time, at least in the inner Solar System, which reduces the impact of peturbations.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why are laptop speakers so bad and crappy, like there's literally zero bass or mids? Like, why don't manufacturers put better quality speakers in their laptops, or at least make the existing ones sound a bit better?
Answer: There’s an actual physical issue that makes it really hard, which makes it expensive, and therefore not many manufacturers bother. Bass response of a speaker requires a certain amount of air volume inside. A laptop is too small and too full of other necessary components for significant bass response, and in fact even too small for good midrange. There are ways to cheat on the air volume, but they’re difficult to engineer. So most manufacturers, especially at cheaper price points, don’t go all that hard at optimising speaker quality in laptops, aiming for merely OK voice quality (so you can have an understandable conversation in a video conference). Some do care, and have the engineering capability to actually do something, and achieve what is physically possible. That’s still not amazing just due to the physical constraints.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How can you connect an electric guitar directly to a laptop and record without buying an interface or other hardware?
Answer: You’re going to have to BUILD an interface or other hardware. The laptop and guitar don’t have compatible signals. End of story, electronics are required one way or another to convert between them. There are many ways to do it. Some are cheap and pretty good. A bought solution will probably cost less than building one too.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the best way to store a guitar in its case to prevent the neck from hitting the lid?
Answer: If the case allows that to happen, throw it out and buy a decent one. Any well-designed case will protect the neck properly when closed. The guitar should not move in the case when it is closed.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Has the electric guitar reached its peak in terms of sound and playability, or is it still evolving as an instrument?
Answer: It’s still evolving. But, like all mature technologies, it’s evolving slower now. This is a recent evolution: (Strandberg Boden 8) This has quite a few unconventional features, including 8 strings, blade pickups, fan frets, and a headless setup with zero fret. But the shape allows playability that is in some ways better than the classic shapes. There are a lot of players who wouldn’t consider one, though, as they are trying to perform music written 50 years ago on instruments like the original performers were using. It’s fine to do that, of course.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What makes steel a unique material for making guitar strings compared to other metals like bronze, copper, and brass?
Answer: For acoustic guitar, it’s not. It’s simply convenient. Acoustic guitar strings can be made of many materials, bronze is commercially available for example. Copper is not strong enough, and brass is too brittle. However, electric guitars require a string that is ferromagnetic. So strings, at least the cores of them, have to be made of steel, certain cobalt alloys, or other even more exotic materials (neodymium, for example). Steel has excellent mechanical properties for the purpose, and is cheaper than the alternatives.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the difference between using fwrite and directly writing into a file handle in C language? Which method is faster and why?
Answer: fwrite is standard C, file handles are an operating system concept and not part of the language standard. Which is faster depends on factors well beyond what the question asks, most critically which OS and which compiler, but also on versions of both, the target hardware, the filesystem where the file resides, system configuration, and more.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why is it recommended to start with a language like Python instead of C/C++ for those who want to become "real" programmers rather than just hobbyists or web developers?
Answer: You have several difficult things to learn at once: Using a relatively straightforward language at the beginning helps reduce the level of confusion and therefore makes the learning curve a bit more manageable. But, in order to learn how to learn languages, pretty quickly you want to pick up another language or three. Then later, learn other languages as required. It will be required, you’ll need quite a few as time goes by. By the way… dismiss the concept that hobbyists and web developers are not “real” programmers. Fine if that’s not where you want to go, but bear in mind that hobbyists have created some amazing and important tools, and web development is paid fairly well for a reason. Also, there’s no such thing as “C/C++”. C and C++ are quite similar, but they are different, and knowledge transfers less than you would expect.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How do hydrogen car engines work? Why have they not been widely used in mass-produced vehicles?
Answer: The best way to use hydrogen in a vehicle is to use a fuel cell. That’s essentially a battery that reacts a chemical fuel, the hydrogen, with oxygen from the air, and uses the electricity generated to run an electric car. It’s quite possible to build the fuel cells and drive system, and they work fine. It’s very expensive, but would come down if made in quantity. That’s not going to happen though, because the fuel is hydrogen. Hydrogen is a terrible fuel. It’s a gas, only liquefies at really super low temperatures so you can’t practically store it that way, diffuses through most materials, makes most metals brittle, has an enormous range of explosive mixtures with air, and burns with a nearly invisible flame. But the worst thing about hydrogen is that you have to make it. The limits on the efficiency of that mean that you only get at most about a third of the energy you put in to the process back out. You can’t do it at home due to the expense and hazards, either. Meanwhile, electric vehicles are about 85% efficient, or even slightly better. So why bother with the difficult, expensive, and dangerous hydrogen, when you can use much less difficult, less expensive, and much less dangerous batteries to get more than twice as much work for the same cost in power? Especially when the electrical distribution system is mostly already there, aside from some adapters and the last couple of meters? That meant that there was no financially sound case for investing in hydrogen production for vehicle fuel, nor in hydrogen filling stations. That meant no case for investing in the technology for filling stations either. So if you have a hydrogen car, you have nowhere to fill it. Not very practical. Now, “green hydrogen” as an investment actually does make sense… hydrogen is used in a whole lot of chemical and industrial processes where there is no substitute, and historically it has mostly been made from natural gas. But vehicle fuel is not a sensible market. By the way, a gasoline or diesel vehicle also used more than enough electricity in refining and distrubuting the fuel to just run an electric vehicle to do the same job… but at least they’re cheap and fairly safe. This, however, is why in the long run they’re going to become much less common.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Are business class seats really that much more comfortable than economy?
Answer: Oh yes. Especially on really long flights (12 hours and longer), where a lie-flat seat lets you sleep. It’s not that good of a bed, but it’s way better than an economy seat. Also, the food is much better, and there’s never a long queue for the toilets. Now imagine flying from New Zealand to Europe via Singapore. 12 hours to Singapore, then a two hour stop, then another 12 hours to somewhere in Europe. If you don’t sleep for that, you’re useless when you arrive, and have to spend at least a day, probably two, recovering from the trip. Whereas in business class, you can be functional the next day, with a bit of practice. However… if your time isn’t that precious, you can achieve the same effect by stopping for a while half way. Even a 12 hour layover is enough, if you book a hotel room in the terminal… and that solution is a lot cheaper.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What causes propeller planes to pitch their nose up when slowing down? Is this the case for all propeller planes?
Answer: All planes do this to some extent, regardless of what kind of propulsion they use. To balance the weight of the plane at a different speed, you need a different angle of attack; if you are slowing down but remaining in level flight, that means the angle of attack has to increase, which means the nose must come up. Maybe not by enough for a passenger to notice, but the change will be there.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can you use a business class lounge if you’re flying economy?
Answer: If you have status with the airline, yes. Sometimes, if you have status with one of their partners. Generally that means either buying in to their frequent flyer club, or by flying enough that you accrue enough status through travel. Either way, you have to have already spent a fair bit of money with the airline.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to make an airplane entirely out of aluminum? Would it be more cost-effective than using composites for some parts?
Answer: Most aircraft from about the 1940s till the 1980s were entirely aluminium. Most aircraft are still at least mostly aluminium. What is more cost effective, like everything else in aviation, depends on the design goals for the particular aircraft.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do airlines prefer to use Boeing or Airbus planes in long haul flights?
Answer: Airlines prefer using the airplane that’s going to make them the most money, they guess. Of course it’s a guess, as it is hard to predict exactly what things will cost over the life of an airplane. But that’s why most airlines run mixed fleets; they decide on routes, then decide what will be the best aircraft for each of them, given their specific circumstances. Then they look at all their routes and decide on the fewest different types that will do acceptably well on all of them. Sometimes that’s only one, but usually it’s a few. Having fewer types in the fleet reduces maintenance and training costs. The manufacturer makes less difference than adding more types to the fleet, though, which is why larger airlines usually have some of each major manufacturer.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why are some airports unable to land big planes like Boeing's 777 and Airbus' A380?
Answer: Usually space on the airport, sometimes the strength of the runway or ramp areas, sometimes the surrounding terrain. Those planes need a minimum length and width of runway, a minimum width of taxiway, a space at the gate or ramp parking of a certain size, and in the case of the A380, special jetways. There’s also a requirement for enough jet blast mitigation, one way or another. They’re incredibly heavy, and the runway, ramp, and taxiways have to be able to withstand the tyre pressure of a plane that large. Especially, the touchdown zone has to be strong enough to have the plane dropped on it, and the surface has to be able to spin up those huge tyres without being stripped off. There are some airports that are known to be able to deal with the airplane in an emergency, but won’t take them in normal operation, often because the runway will take one landing, then will need repairs before it can be used again. And of course, the airport has to have enough fuel on site to refuel one. In an emergency, that may lead to the aircraft being stranded for a long time while fuel is sourced. Many airports those largest airliners are only permitted to use certain areas that have been prepared for them, including runways. Surrounding terrain becomes a factor because those aircraft are also very fast, and so cannot make particularly tight radius turns. Nor do they climb or descend at particularly steep angles. So it may not be possible to fit an approach or departure path into the airspace within the constraints of normal operations (which are very conservative so that those paths can be flown in emergencies or poor weather).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How can we determine the maximum load capacity of a plane based on its model and weight?
Answer: Find the operation manual for that specific airplane and look up the performance tables and limits. Or, for an approximation, look up the general specs on Wikipedia or the manufacturer’s site.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What happens to your baggage when a flight gets cancelled and you fly home with another airline at no cost?
Answer: When a flight is cancelled and you get rebooked, one of two things happens. Either your baggage is transferred to the new flight as if it were an ordinary transfer, or you get your baggage from the claim and re-check it. If this actually happens, you’ll be told which it is going to be. I’ve had it go both ways. Usually the first if the new flight leaves from the same terminal. If the new flight is going to be a lot later, they usually have you collect your baggage, both because the terminal has limited storage, and because you will probably appreciate a change of clothes and access to your other personal stuff.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a chance that the US air force has a simulation designed to come up with the safest route possible for a military jet to follow to avoid enemy radars by flying at certain altitudes and certain land objects like roads and certain geography?
Answer: I’m sure they do, it’s such an obvious idea. It’s not even that hard as software goes, though getting the calibration data for some of the models would be expensive.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: In shortest-path graph algorithms, why do we typically use a "visited list" instead of adding a boolean "visited" property to the node class and setting it when we visit the node? Wouldn't this save space?
Answer: For one of several reasons: Which it is depends on the algorithm and implementation.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to see Venus without a telescope? If so, why do people often recommend using a telescope to view it?
Answer: You can see it very easily if you know where and when to look. But to the naked eye it looks much like a very bright star. Some people have sharp enough eyes to see that it isn’t a star directly (I can see its phases, just barely), but most people don’t. Whereas, look at it through a telescope and it is instantly obvious that it’s a planet. So while you don’t need a telescope to tell there’s something there, you get a much better view with one.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can we see a planet-sized object in space without using any equipment, such as telescopes?
Answer: Many of the planets were discovered before the telescope. So, obviously yes. Of course, it has to be large enough and close enough, but that does apply to Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, all of which can be seen with your own eyes if you have dark-ish skies and know where to look. And… the Moon is almost planet-sized, and that’s real obvious because it’s so close (in space terms).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If airline baggage cannot travel unaccompanied, how do airlines return it to me when they lose or misdirect it? Is it re-checked to travel on a cargo service?
Answer: They’ll put it on one or more of their own flights as baggage, and then courier it or use a taxi to get it to you at your destination. But… before that, it will be inspected way more thoroughly than ordinary baggage, precisely because it is now unaccompanied. The rule is actually there so people don’t check in baggage containing a bomb and then no-show for the flight, so that the only bombers that will blow up flights are suiciders (there are of course other measures to help stop them). Given that you showed up and had no way of knowing your baggage wasn’t on the flight, that’s not you, but nevertheless they’re going to take a look at the bag. It can also happen that your itinerary catches up with the bag before the airline locates it. Once many years ago I was travelling with a group of coworkers around the US, and at one transfer in Atlanta some of our gear didn’t come with us. We didn’t need it at our next destination anyway, but the airline didn’t find it. As it happens we travelled back through Atlanta a few days later, and went to the baggage office during the layover just in case. Well, lo and behold, the case was there, they just hadn’t got to the point of redirecting it yet. So we claimed it and it travelled on with us.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do private companies offer helicopter flights similar to plane flights?
Answer: Yes. Many of them, there are probably several in most sizeable cities.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the reason for aircraft using propellers instead of jet engines? Is it due to noise levels?
Answer: Jets and propellers have different pros and cons. When designing a plane, the designer has to have a goal in mind; it’s not possible to be good at everything. If one of the goals is being able to use short runways, for example, you want propellers instead of jets, because they work better at low speeds and therefore give much better acceleration on takeoff. The tradeoff is of course that jets work much better at high speeds, so if your goal is going fast propellers may not be suitable; if you want to go supersonic, jets are the only realistic option (at least until you want to go so fast your best option is a rocket). Small turbine engines are horrifyingly inefficient, so if the aircraft is going to need less than about 400 horsepower, you want to use propellers and piston engines (or propellers and electric motors), because a jet is going to have ridiculous fuel consumption. You might use a turboprop for reliability or weight reasons, though. By the way, this is also why we don’t drive turbine cars. For small airliners, turboprops and jets overlap in capabilities, but for the same number of seats the jet will be faster for long routes, the turboprop will be faster for short ones. For many routes where the flight times are about the same, the turboprop will do it cheaper. The jet will need more runway, and also will climb and descend at shallower angles, so the turboprop will be able to use small airports and mountain airports that the jet can’t. The turboprop may also be able to carry quite a lot more weight, which makes them good for cargo. For really huge planes, though, jets are better, because there’s a limit to how big you can reasonably build a propeller. There is for a jet too, but it’s a lot larger.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can a plane be made entirely with electric power? If so, what would be the estimated cost of building one?
Answer: Not only can it be done, it has been. That’s a Pipistrel Velis Electro, which is in series production. As for price… yours for US $117,000. It’s not the only one, either.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How can you turn the wheel of a car without power steering if you are out of fuel and unable to push start the engine or use starting fluid?
Answer: Muscles. Power steering doesn’t completely stop working without power assist, it just gets harder to turn. At highway speed, the power assist isn’t really doing anything much in most cars, you only really notice it when going slowly, or especially trying to turn the steering when stationary. This is a very good thing if your hydraulic fluid leaks out while moving, obviously.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to compile UNIX utilities such as diff or less from source to run under MS DOS 6.22?
Answer: Not from the Unix source. MS DOS doesn’t have most of the APIs the Unix utilities use. There’s often something equivalent, but completely different in the details. There are ports of many of the Unix utilities to DOS, however. Some programs may have both ports in the same source tree, with preprocessor definitions separating the two sets of code.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why can't airplanes use reverse thrust to power out of the gate?
Answer: Some can, but it is almost never done. That’s because it’s not safe; there’s always a lot of people and clutter around gates, and reverse thrust from a jet backing out is more than enough jet blast to pick up baggage carts and throw them around. So the liklihood of someone getting hurt, equipment getting damaged, and even damage to the terminal building and injuries inside is too high to accept. Besides, it’s a waste of fuel.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the process of replacing all of the frets on an acoustic or electric guitar?
Answer: First consider whether the existing ones just need re-dressing, because that is far less work. There’s a note in the middle of the steps where you skip to for that. Then basically: Now you see why a technician or luthier will charge quite a bit for this service. Also note that you can buy a decent guitar for the price of the tools, and a guitar’s worth of fretwire costs around $70. So most of the cost is labour… and there’s a lot of it.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why are fighter planes designed with such high consoles and poor forward vision?
Answer: It’s pretty simple… you don’t actually need to be able to see forward much below horizontal when flying a plane. Anything that is in that direction you will have to roll the plane to point it there anyway, because you can’t really push into downward turns well, so it’s not important. Fighters have excellent visibility to the sides, upwards, and behind. That’s because those are the directions that matter… the plane can turn toward those directions quickly. And if you really do need to look at something that is hidden by the plane… just roll it over. That way you’ll be prepositioned to point at it if you need to. Even given all that… the forward vision in a fighter is still way, way, way better than in most other airplanes.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to tune a stringed instrument once and never have to tune it again?
Answer: No, but pianos often stay pretty decently in tune for a few years in people’s homes. Tuning isn’t hard, takes a couple of minutes at most, and is quite important. Also, once you get in to reasonably high level performance, you will need to tweak your tuning for different performances, as there is no fixed ideal tuning anyway. This is why guitarists have so many instruments… each is set up for different tunings, sometimes for individual songs.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why do airplanes only use flaps for landing and not for takeoff? Do flaps help with lift and reducing drag during both phases of flight?
Answer: Airplanes do use flaps for both landing and takeoff. Also, flaps do not decrease drag, entirely the opposite. However, the flap settings used for takeoff are usually a lot less than is used for landing. Flaps increase lift, but they also increase drag. At higher flap settings, the drag increases very quickly, more than the lift. So… when landing, you want to be able to fly slowly to reduce how much runway you need, and more drag just helps you slow down. Therefore you use the most flap you can, usually. Whereas, when taking off, you want to slow down the speed you require to fly, for sure, but you also want less drag so it takes less time (and therefore distance) to accelerate to that speed. This results in less flap being optimal for takeoff distance. On some aircraft where flaps will deploy quickly you might even start the roll with no flaps and add them part way down the runway. Too much flap would also make it hard to climb after takeoff.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Have we considered electric trucks to intelligently go eco-friendly?
Answer: Yes. Electric trucks are fairly hard, and so far haven’t made a massive impact. Part of the problem is that the trucking industry is structured around the capabilities of diesel trucks. It’s also very different around the world, so one size does not fit all. But give it time. There is a case for electric trucks, and the issues are being solved. The same applies to buses, only it’s rather easier, and so there are a lot of electric buses around the world already.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a belief that Go language will eventually replace Java and C++? Are there any perceived advantages of Go language over these languages?
Answer: No. Originally the designers of Go had replacing C (not C++) in mind. But as the language developed, it has turned out to be more suitable as a replacement for Python. Go is a pretty decent language, but it turns out to be best for small to medium sized or loosely coupled applications, much like Python. It’s also not really suitable for kernel-like situations, so it can’t replace C there. There are a lot of system management and monitoring utilities written in Go (Prometheus, many parts of Kubernetes), and development of new applications of that sort in Python has basically stopped.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it safe to use a bass head for a guitar, or vice versa? Will it cause any damage to the electronics inside the head?
Answer: Bass amps for guitar: fine. Might not sound great, might be awesome, but you won’t hurt anything. Some guitarists, especially if they are using 7 or more strings, do this by preference. If you play both, find a bass amp that does well for guitar and you only need one amp. Some guitar amps will not handle bass, though. You’re at risk of damaging the speakers, even if you use bass speakers (the electronics should be fine). OK if you play very quietly, but not safe for anything more than home practice or testing to see if an instrument works.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: As a starship and the booster has lots of engines, if one fails, why don't they just use a different engine? Or fire more at low power then power up one to full power if one fails. They have lots of spares.
Answer: That is precisely what they do; start them all (starting is a bit complicated, and easier to do for the booster on the pad), and plan the flight such that either a bit more power or a longer burn will deal with engine failures. There is of course a limit to how many of each type of engine can fail and in what arrangements, but the rocket is designed to tolerate a certain number of failures.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the significance of a double underscore in C++?
Answer: Nothing in particular in the language itself. Many programs and libraries use it at the beginning of names to denote a name that is not part of the public interface, but nevertheless has to be public for technical reasons. It’s also common practice in the naming of ‘helper functions’ in some code bases. In general, it shows that the name in question is a bit special, probably intended to be restricted in some way, and you should look up or figure out how that naming convention is being used in this particular code.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to use an unmodified SpaceX Starship as a space station after it has landed on Mars or another planet?
Answer: That’s the plan for how to use Starship in those roles. A Starship to be used like that will be built for the purpose, with suitable facilities inside. Then it will be used as transport for the crew, accommodation on site, and their return vehicle. Which means that any major maintenance and refits can be done on Earth, rather than in space, which is a whole lot easier. Other Starships will be essentially buildings to be flown in to position and then left there.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why do universities teach C and C++, though they are regarded as the most difficult languages and there are better alternatives? C and C++ aren’t expanding and will be dead in 30 years, but Stanford, Harvard and U Mich use C++ as a primary language.
Answer: It comes down to this: a bachelors degree is a qualification that says “I can do the standard hard stuff that is required in this field”. That’s the point. A Masters says “I can do hard stuff in this field even if the book hasn’t been written yet” and a PhD says “I can invent how to do hard stuff in this field when nobody has before” (and a Doctorate says “I invented the field”). So a university that doesn’t teach a commonly used difficult technique just because it is difficult is failing the students badly. C and C++ will not be dead in 30 years. There’s a simple reason for that: it is pretty much certain that the operating system kernel on your personal devices is mostly written in those two languages, no matter what devices you have. There will be traces of others, but the bulk will be either C or C++. That moves relatively slowly, so while Linux and Windows (for example) are both gaining Rust code in the kernel, that very likely will not be even close to the majority in that time frame. So if you don’t understand the basics of C and C++, you don’t understand how computers work… and computer science is a degree in exactly that. Now, you don’t have to teach those languages as a first language, and probably shouldn’t, but you do have to teach them.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How can the International Space Station be seen from Earth? Do we need a special instrument to view it?
Answer: You need a clear, dark sky, and a satellite tracking app on your phone to know when and where to look. It’s very easy to see, no optical instruments required. Most nights that are clear enough you have a chance or two to see it. There are usually plenty of other orbiting objects you can spot with one of those apps too. Sometimes you can see other spacecraft on approach or departing from the ISS, which is particularly cool. That takes some organisation, though, as there’s a narrow time window when this is possible.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What are the steps to becoming a top-level quantum physicist without any connections in the field?
Answer: Learn your physics. Make the connections. End of story. There is no easy way, and no way of turning a career into a series of easy steps. That said, the next step is usually fairly clear once you are in to the process. So, first step, go to a decent university and learn your physics. While there, ask the professors and any visitors who come around what their career path has been like. You’ll start to see options for your own next step. As it happens, my obvious next step at one point took me right off the physics career path and into computers.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why can't the body of a plane be square?
Answer: It can: Thing is, that’s a small-ish plane (ten seats), not pressurised, and not particularly fast. The faster and higher you want to go, the more a smoothly curving shape has advantages in efficiency: the pressurisation wants the shape to be round anyway, so if the natural shape is close to round, you need less material to keep the air in. As well, a round tube makes less drag and more lift, both of which are good for going fast. Just about any question about airplanes comes down to: that’s how you get the cheapest overall airplane that can do whatever the designers wanted it to do. The differences then mostly come down to what the designers wanted. In the case of the Airvan, they wanted something that can use short-ish runways and carry nine people plus a pilot cheaply over relatively short distances, while making it easy for everyone to see what is on the ground or water underneath. It works great for that (ugly, but very comfortable, relatively quiet, and apparently has nice handling). High speed and high altitude were not necessary.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for an airplane to have triangular wings? If not, what are the reasons?
Answer: It’s possible. It’s unusual, because it’s best for supersonic flight. So it’s mostly used for military airplanes.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to land without glide slope in real life aviation, or is it only achievable in flight simulators?
Answer: Yes, and every pilot knows how. What isn’t possible is doing that when you can’t see the runway. One way or another you need precision vertical guidance, and there’s only three ways to do that: visual, ILS, or GPS. The latter two use the glide slope, and work in poor visibility. Visual landings without glide slope are entirely normal, and very common.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for someone to fly a plane with their family on board?
Answer: Sure. I’ve even done it. Well, only some of the family, but close enough. You just need access to a plane and a suitable license.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the process for landing a helicopter without the rotors turning?
Answer: Crash. If the rotors ever slow below a certain minimum speed (which is specific to the type of helicopter), that’s a guaranteed crash. So stopped is certainly much too slow. Even letting them get significantly slowed down from normal speed is a serious problem if you are too low and slow to get them back up to normal speed. So… there is no such procedure, instead the pilot must manage rotor RPM at all times, within quite tight bounds, even after an engine failure. Fortunately most helicopters have systems to help with that, so it’s not actually that hard.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why is it necessary to switch your mobile to flight mode when boarding a plane? Can't the internet be shut down in that area like it is during an earthquake?
Answer: The issue with shutting down the cells is this: all that does is makes everyone’s phone try even harder to contact a cell. So instead of chatting away at relatively low volume, they start shouting. It’s necessary because there is a small chance of bad behaviour in the airplane’s electronics due to interference from phones. Unlikely, but definitely possible, and the aviation industry is extremely careful with safety. It’s very easy to demonstrate the issue with an older model light airplane, by the way, and I have done so myself. Airliners are more robust, but it can still happen.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it true that airplanes are designed to fly upside down using the same principles as flying right-side up?
Answer: Those airplanes where flying upside down (called inverted) is any kind of consideration for the designers at all, yes, fly using exactly the same principles. It’s usually not nearly as efficient as upright flight, because even planes that can don’t spend much time doing that, so optimising for the normal situation makes sense. That doesn’t mean it couldn’t be equally as efficient, just that doing so is not a priority, and the difference in fuel consumption when you just want to go somewhere is quite large.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can an aircraft be controlled by multiple pilots using VR technology or a similar method from outside of the aircraft?
Answer: Yes. But… not particularly safely. The problem is this: we don’t have a sufficiently reliable way to communicate with an aircraft in flight. The risk is acceptable in military drone missions, and for small civilian drones, but not for a lot of applications.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the thickest string on a bass guitar?
Answer: It’s whichever one has the lowest pitch. In standard tuning, with 4 strings it’s an E, and on 5s and 6s it’s the B below that. But unusual tunings are pretty common.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How long can a guitar be left untouched before the strings go out of tune and need to be changed? Do they stay in tune forever if stored away?
Answer: They don’t stay in tune for ever, you’ll have to retune before using it again. What makes strings unusable is their physical condition, which only really changes due to wear from use and corrosion. But… the strings remain in usable condition for months at least, and if the humidity is low so they don’t rust, years. Bass strings last much longer; potentially decades.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the purpose of the white spirals painted around jet engine nacelles? Do they help reduce bird strikes?
Answer: I don’t know about bird strikes, but what they do is reduce accidents among ground staff at the airports. Jet engines will turn in the wind if the oil is hot enough, and in warm weather that is possible for at least half an hour after shutdown (maybe longer). Without that spiral, it’s hard to tell if an engine is just turning in the wind or actually running, especially at night under lights that flicker. An engine turning in the wind is no problem to walk in front of, but a running engine is extremely dangerous, even if it is just idling.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a universal size for guitar necks and bodies, or does each guitar body require a specific type of neck to be attached?
Answer: There’s no universal size. For some guitar models, necks aren’t even interchangeable, and you have to adjust the body or add shims to match them. Some manufacturers partially standardise on a neck pocket design, so you can frankenstein the ‘wrong’ neck onto a body (Fender and Ibanez both do this to some extent).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it necessary for all solid body electric guitars to be routed for pickups and electronics?
Answer: The pickups and electronics are what make it an electric guitar. However, routing out a solid block of wood to make spaces to install them is not the only way to go about mounting them. For example… you could make an open-frame instrument with the pickups on sliding rails: Or you could surface mount them: (there is no cavity under that pickup, just some screw holes and one for the wiring)

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: For any pilots, is doing just a PPL a good way for me to gauge if I should go ahead with a CPL and take on flying as my career?
Answer: It’s a good thing to do for many reasons, as the things you learn about yourself will be valuable in almost everything you do later. It also improves your driving a lot, which may one day save your life. It will tell you if you enjoy the reality of operating airplanes. But what it won’t tell you is the reality of being a professional pilot. You will, however, be interacting frequently with your instructors and the aviation community, so you’ll have the chance to go ask those questions. I wasn’t intending to fly for a living, though I’d love to be able to do a CPL one day, so I didn’t do very much of that. But it’s very clear that just the pilot training doesn’t tell you what aviation is like as a job.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to tune an electric guitar to the same strings as an acoustic guitar? Are they essentially the same instrument?
Answer: It’s not just possible, it’s normal. Standard tuning is the same, and it’s actually possible to use electric guitar strings on a steel-string acoustic (though not necessarily optimal). They are not quite the same instrument, though. There are technique differences and many things to learn switching between them. They’re just extremely closely related. BTW, many people assume you should learn acoustic first. This is not true, you should learn whichever you most want to play in the long run first. Acoustic is not easier, it’s just different, and cheap electric guitars are better than cheap acoustics, even though you need an amp (or some substitute) as well for the electric.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it harmful to leave electric or acoustic guitars in their cases for extended periods of time, such as overnight?
Answer: Much less harmful than leaving them out. Instruments are fragile, and accidents happen. Instruments can stay in their cases for decades and be unharmed, other than corrosion of metal parts (especially strings). I don’t recommend you do this, checking on it occasionally is better, but it’s usually OK anyway. Take the instrument out to play it, put it back in the case when you’re done.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do electric guitars need to mimic the form of classical guitar? Do we have minimalist electric guitars?
Answer: No, they don’t have to be particularly close to a classical guitar (and most aren’t). I’d call this minimalist, though it’s not particularly ergonomic (Steinberger Spirit): Something like this will be much more comfortable to play (Strandberg Boden): (the frets really aren’t parallel, this is a mild multiscale guitar) Or even more extreme (Ormsby Goliath): Those last two are about the minimal electric guitar shape consistent with being comfortable to play; they have structure in the places necessary to support the instrument and the player’s arm, and strap buttons in the places needed for balance, and everything unnecessary has been removed.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for a private pilot without an instrument rating to rent and fly an aircraft in instrument flight rules (IFR) conditions?
Answer: If you’re capable of doing that without killing yourself, it’s not going to be much trouble to get the rating. The average survival time of an unqualified pilot finding themselves in actual IFR is a couple of minutes. Don’t even think about it if you’re not qualified. So… possible, yes, but it’s a complicated way to suicide. It’s also illegal.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can I be a commercial pilot in Australia with a level 2 autism?
Answer: I can’t give you a definitive answer, but I can tell you how to find out for sure. That is, collect all the documentation you have about your health, including the autism diagnosis, but everything else as well (recent blood tests, whatever you have). Then, write a nice letter to an Aviation Medical Examiner explaining what you want to know and that you have the information, and would they be willing to answer the question for you. There’s a list of those people at Once you find one who is willing, send them the info, and make an appointment with them if they ask for one. This will probably cost something, but it will cost a lot less than getting part way through the licensing process and finding out that you can’t get a medical certificate. If they’d be prepared to issue a private certificate but not a commercial one, or they wouldn’t issue any certificate, well, at least then you know.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: In what situations do airlines use manual flying instead of auto-pilot?
Answer: Autoland and automatic taxi are only used when they have to be to be, either dictated by conditions, or because the crew need the practice to retain their currency in the procedure. That’s because the autoland procedures are more work than just landing the plane. Also, sometimes ATC may not be prepared to grant a clearance for an autoland approach if the conditions don’t require it, because it adds to their workload too. Given that, airlines use autopilot as much as possible. No matter how good a pilot is at hand flying, autopilot uses less fuel, so it saves money. Even on autopilot, the crew have to constantly monitor what is going on. Autopilot reduces their workload some of the time, but there is always attention given to the progress of the flight. The result is: many short flights are entirely manual, nearly all taxi, takeoffs, and landings are manual, but most of the time airliners are on autopilot, especially jets. It’s unusual to be on autopilot with wheels down, but normal with them up.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to use pure oxygen as a fuel source for jet engines instead of kerosene? Would this method be more efficient?
Answer: Not instead of. Oxygen doesn’t burn in air, as it is an oxidiser not a fuel, and it happens that Earth has an oxidising atmosphere (due to containing a lot of, you guessed it, oxygen). But as well as kerosene? Well, then you get this: A rocket is in many ways just a jet engine that carries its own oxidiser along with it.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the purpose of a hood on a car? Why are engines on planes exposed?
Answer: The hood keeps weather and debris off the engine, and plays an important part in pedestrian safety too (yes, cars are designed with what happens if you hit a pedestrian in mind). It also keeps some of the noise inside. Airplane engines mostly are not exposed, it’s just that the engine cowlings (which are what the equivalent parts on an airplane are called) don’t make that quite so obvious. For example, here’s a 1970s Piper Cherokee engine with the cowling open: Here’s much the same view of the left engine on a Boeing 737: Obviously that one is a little bigger…

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What are the reasons for not replacing car engines with more efficient options such as turbines or electric motors?
Answer: Turbines are not more efficient at car scale; for really huge machines, such as airliners, ships, and locomotives they can be very efficient, but the efficiency drops as the turbine gets smaller. So while it is entirely possible to build a turbine car, the fuel economy will suck. Turbines also won’t be nice to drive in a car, because they have quite slow throttle response. Electric motors… that’s down to batteries and places to charge. We’re getting there with that, but any such transition takes a lot of time.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Are all commercial planes controlled by fly-by-wire systems or are there still some that use manual controls for their flight surfaces? If so, which ones still use manual controls?
Answer: There are more commercial aircraft that do not use fly-by-wire than those that do. Of course, commercial aircraft includes a lot more than just airliners. Fly by wire is basically nonexistent in anything smaller than about 30 seats, except perhaps a few high-end business jets. But even with airliners, it’s not universal, even in brand new airplanes. It is true that the largest new airliners are all fly-by-wire, now that the 747 is retired. 777, 787, A350, A380… all FBW.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If an IP address of someone says the USA, does that mean they are in the US or could they still be overseas?
Answer: They are most likely in the US, but could be anywhere. IP address location is not, and never will be, anything like reliable. IP addresses are about which organisation you are using to connect to the Internet. So, for example, if you’re in an office of a US corporation somewhere outside the US, the building network may well be using company addresses, and location may get the wrong answer. And that’s just one of many ways this can go wrong.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How did mathematicians demonstrate that the square root of -1 is possible to do? What is the logic behind it? How do we obtain a negative number doing a^2?
Answer: It’s more a case of… someone thought, well, what would happen if we could do that? If you work through the consequences of being able to take square roots of negative numbers, it turns out to be massively useful. But you’re correct, in the sense that it simply doesn’t work with the kinds of numbers you’re used to. So it isn’t a matter of demonstrating possibility, it’s a matter of, suppose we can. That’s because to do this, we have to define a new kind of number where it is possible. The only reason we go there, though, is because complex numbers are so incredibly useful that we can’t build the modern world without them. Anything to do with AC electricity, including mains power, audio, radio, radar, WiFi, 5G, and so many others, uses complex numbers in the standard way of analysing how it works… and for good reason, it helps a great deal with managing the messy math. Similarly optics. And complex numbers are so fundamental to quantum mechanics you’d have a terrible time trying to work without them. So… suspend disbelief, you’ll see what’s on the other side, and then it will seem far more reasonable.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the process for checking luggage at the airport when flying internationally? How much time does it typically take for them to inspect everything?
Answer: Exactly like a domestic flight: show up at checkin, either use a kiosk and tag your own, or go to an agent and get them to tag it. Inspections are part of the checkin time, and also part of the time it takes to get your luggage at the far end. You don’t need to think about it, except to show up on time and find out how long you can expect to wait for baggage at a particular airport, if that is going to matter. It often takes longer to get yourself through the process than for your bags anyway; wait time for baggage on international flights is usually short.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If DNS uses UDP rather than TCP, and DNS responses are often too long to fit in one UDP packet, how does DNS protocol make sure the packets come in the same order as they are sent?
Answer: It doesn’t. DNS can use TCP, and every server must support TCP, it just uses UDP by default since most queries fit in a single packet. If a DNS server has a response that is too large, it sends back a partial response and a flag that says that the response is truncated. Sometimes what the client wants is in the partial response and it won’t bother to retry, but if it does need the rest it will try again using TCP. If a client expects a large response, it can try the first query using TCP.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is an IP address based on location or device?
Answer: Neither, but it’s more like location. What it actually is based on is who owns the address block that your network is connected to. This is usually an ISP, but at work may be your employer, and university networks usually own their own addresses too. Knowing physically where that might be is challenging, though there are data sources for that which are frequently updated to be roughly accurate. They can never be perfect, but they’re good enough to be useful since most networks don’t move around much. So, for example, while I worked for Google anything on the office network used Google addresses. They did actually geolocate correctly, but that’s because it’s Google and they run a geolocation service and therefore have people to make sure that works. My previous employer was a Japanese company, and sometimes our New Zealand office would geolocate to Tokyo. The IETF itself is a fun case… that’s the organisation that made these rules in the first place, and so it has its own address block. But that network only exists for a few weeks a year, and it moves around, so quite often you show up to a meeting in, say, London, and some devices think they are wherever the last meeting was… in this case, Yokohama.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do turboprops reduce vibration compared to standard jet engines on propeller-driven airplanes? If not, why do many smaller commercial airlines use turboprops instead of jets?
Answer: Turboprops have some advantages, but lower vibration isn’t one of them. Turboprops: For long flights, jets are better, but for short routes, a turboprop can be competitive.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the difference in tone between an upright bass and a double bass?
Answer: There isn’t one, they’re different names for the same instrument. There are different tones available, however. Plywood and carved basses have different sounds. Not that one is better than the other, though carved is much more expensive, it depends on what you want to play; ply is definitely better for rockabilly and similar styles, and has a place in jazz too. Which strings you use makes a really significant difference, and so does the setup of the instrument. Steel versus aramid versus nylon cores, and what the wrapping materials are, makes an enormous difference (personally, I like aramid/tungsten alloy/nickel alloy strings, but that’s just me).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why are they called "guitar" strings instead of "bass" strings? Do bass guitars have thicker and longer strings compared to other instruments with this name?
Answer: The names of these instruments are extremely confusing. There are more or less four kinds of guitar: classical, flamenco, steel string acoustic, and electric. Electric guitars use similar strings to steel string acoustic. Confusingly, electric guitar strings must be made of either steel or cobalt; steel string acoustic guitars can use a much wider range of materials, and in particular do not have to use steel. There are, however, strings that can be used on either steel string or electric guitars. Classical and flamenco guitars use gut, nylon, or various other polymer strings, the low strings are wound with bronze, silver, or occasionally stainless steel wire. There are also lap steel guitars, but I’m not convinced they’re actually guitars. They’re kind of something else. Electric bass isn’t a guitar. It was developed to be a louder double bass. Of course, electric bass has a lot in common with electric guitar; they’re clearly related too. But it’s a different instrument. Most electric basses have to use steel or cobalt strings like an electric guitar… but only most, some use laser or piezo pickups and can use other materials too. Acoustic bass guitar is actually based on the electric bass, and also isn’t a guitar. Yes, even though it’s right there in the common name. It’s called that to distinguish it from the double bass (which isn’t a violin either, but that’s a whole essay all of it’s own). Acoustic bass guitar strings are usually bronze wrapped steel. Double bass strings can be made from a huge variety of weird materials, and the construction is radically different from any guitar string (as is true for any other bowed instrument as well). In any case… strings for a low-pitched instrument with a roughly 34″ scale length are much longer and much heavier than strings for a higher pitched instrument with a 25.5″ scale length. So much so that there’s absolutely no way the wrong strings will fit on either instrument.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the difference between a Nikon and Sigma lens when it comes to image quality and sharpness?
Answer: The quality range overlaps so much that you cannot say anything based on the brand; you have to look at specific lenses. Both companies make some of the best lenses in existence, but it is often the case that one or the other is clearly ahead for a specific application. I have owned both, though my current kit is all Nikon. I would buy another Sigma if it turned out that it would be better for what I had in mind; it just hasn’t happened since I bought the Z series.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is the size and weight of big HiFi speakers causing them to become obsolete?
Answer: I don’t think so. I think it’s more about social expectations and the way people listen to music. Listening on speakers takes over the entire room, maybe the entire house, and if you live in an apartment will probably annoy the neighbours. People used to listen socially, and you’d hang out in groups listening to the same thing. Headphones or earbuds keep your music to you. Music outside of live performance has become a private thing. You can, of course, still get speakers, because some people do like them, but I doubt they’ll return to as mainstream of an item as they were in the 1980s and earlier.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the reason behind Nikon not developing a mirrorless camera that is as good as their DSLR cameras?
Answer: Why would they bother? Their mirrorless cameras are better than the DSLRs. Or at least, the latest modesl are; the Z f, Z 8, and Z 9 are clearly better than any of the DSLRs, and the earlier and low end models are debatable, but also very respectable cameras given their feature sets and pricing.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What are the key differences between DSLR and mirrorless cameras, and which one is better suited for my needs?
Answer: You didn’t tell us what your needs are, so that part of the question is unanswerable. However. The differences are mostly the nature of the viewfinder, and the position of the lens mount. In a DSLR, the viewfinder is optical. It works with the camera switched off. However, it also works using only available light, so focusing at night can be very difficult. Also, the viewfinder can differ slightly from the actual sensor area, because it is a separate optical system. It is almost always smaller, because that reduces the size of the mirror and prisms. The optical viewfinder also requires a mirror box to bounce the light into the viewfinder, which means the sensor to lens mount distance has to be relatively large. A mirrorless has an electronic viewfinder. What you see is being recorded by the actual image sensor. It only works with the camera on. But an electronic viewfinder has auto-exposure, so it works as a night vision device. Focusing in low light is much easier, so is framing your image. The viewfinder can also pull various useful tricks, like highlighting those areas of the image that are in focus, or overexposed. Lacking a mirror box, the lens mount can be much closer to the sensor. This allows mirrorless-specific lenses to have specifications impossible on an SLR… either much smaller and lighter, much faster, or with zoom ranges you could not achieve. This also allows a very broad range of adaptors to SLR lenses, other mirrorless systems, historical lens systems, etc. If you ask which camera from any current maker has the broadest selection of their own lenses that will function on it, the answer is always a recent mirrorless. They tend to be much better than even new DSLRs at working well with very old or unusual lenses. A mirrorless is also often smaller and lighter than a DSLR of similar specification. This is not always a good thing, as this affects the handling and balance of some of the larger lenses. Remember you are buying in to a system, and the most important question here is actually which system has the right lenses for you. Often that will be a mirrorless, because of its broad compatibility and the incredible performance of some of the mirrorless-specific lenses.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do DSLR cameras come with built-in lenses or do they need to be purchased separately?
Answer: Built-in, no. Sold in the same package? Sometimes, that’s called a ‘camera kit’, and the particular lenses in them get called ‘kit lenses’. High end models are often not sold in a kit, low-end models sometimes are not sold without a kit lens. In any case there is little point getting a DSLR or mirrorless with only one lens, so I expect most buyers will get at least one additional lens even if they start with a kit.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the difference in resolution between normal DSLR cameras and mirrorless cameras? How does this affect their image quality?
Answer: There is no inherent difference in resolution. DSLRs and mirrorless cameras use different sensors, and it’s quite possible that there is no exactly corresponding sensor for each type of camera, but that’s an accident of what parts actually exist. The reason for the sensors being different is that a mirrorless camera has to integrate its focus sensors into the image sensor, whereas a DSLR usually has separate focus sensors, although of course some manufacturers have started using mirrorless-style sensors in DSLRs (because they’re better for video). As always in engineering, there are pros and cons to this. Pro: it’s physically impossible for there to be a difference in focus position between the focus and imaging sensors, so the focus will be perfect. Also, you can use the full performance of the focusing system while shooting video. Con: The focus sensors do make a tiny difference to the sensitivity of the imaging pixels where they are, so the sensor has a slight pattern to its sensitivity. But, the pattern is constant, and easily removed in constructing the final image (this is done automatically by the software in the camera, even in RAW, you don’t ever have to think about it). In practice, there is no significant difference in sensor quality, so image quality with identical lenses is pretty much identical, and the mirrorless camera has such an optical advantage that there’s really no contest if you allow purpose-designed lenses (which you should). On top of which, mirrorless cameras are just better to use: smaller, lighter, much wider lens compatibility, viewfinders you can actually use reliably at night, focus peaking in the viewfinder. The con is just shorter battery life, which is completely tolerable with a little planning and a spare battery or two. Some people don’t like the video viewfinder, but most find that very usable with a bit of practice.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How do cameras capture images? Do they use pixels or record light?
Answer: Digital cameras use pixels *to* record light. The camera’s sensor is a pattern, usually a grid, of light-sensitive pixels, each one of which counts the number of photons of light that interact with it. Over those is a grid of colour filters, which make some pixels sensitive to red, some to green, and some to blue. Some sensors have other colours as well. The camera reads out the sensor to get a giant list of how many counts there were for each pixel, and reassembles that with some mathematics into an image file. The actual layout of the sensor can be quite different from what an abstract digital image is supposed to be, so the transformation isn’t necessarily simple. Here’s an extreme close-up image of the corner of a sensor: You can see the colour filters there. This sensor has a fairly common layout, with two green, one red, and one blue filter per final image pixel.

Question: Is it possible to capture a complete image of the Milky Way using a single camera or a mobile phone's camera?
Answer: Yes, but it’s going to involve a bunch of travel, and you’d best invest in a good camera because the travel will be quite expensive.
