Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why do computers use swapping instead of utilizing more RAM, even though it is theoretically faster than disk access?
Answer: Disk and SSD are cheaper and use less power than RAM. For a while recently RAM was also hard to get in large quantities. It’s all about optimising how much performance you get for a given budget. You get different answers if you are optimising for battery life, power consumption, or outright performance, and depending on what applications you expect to run. There have been times when no amount of money could buy you enough RAM, but you could get enough disk, and so you’d just do that and accept that it was going to take a long time to get the computation done.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why would helicopter operators turn off the helicopter's transponder?
Answer: Several reasons. If operating solely on an airfield, for example hover-taxiing the aircraft to get fuel, the transponder isn’t necessary, and it’s polite to turn it off. If the alternator has failed, turning off the transponder lowers the electrical power requirements by a lot, and will result in the battery lasting much longer for more important items. In small aircraft, the transponder is by far the largest power consumer. If the transponder itself has failed. Especially if it’s on fire. If ATC asked for it to be switched off or into a different mode, which they do from time to time. Military and security-related aircraft sometimes don’t want the whole world knowing where they are, so they switch off transponders. They also have a different kind of transponder that civilian aircraft don’t have, the idea being that their own controllers can see them but anybody else has difficulty.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What prevents helicopter rotors from spinning in the wind when the helicopter is stationary?
Answer: There’s a brake on the rotor head, used for exactly this reason, and also to stop the rotors more quickly during shutdown. So, in a sense, a helicopter has a parking brake… even if it has no wheels.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What measures can be taken to prevent an aircraft from stalling during a runway landing without engine power, similar to auto-rotation in helicopters?
Answer: That’s actually pretty straightforward: never try to fly at an angle of attack that is too large. Which amounts to not trying to fly too slow. It’s just like maintaining speed in a powered approach, except that you know you have only the energy you start with. So instead of using power to add energy and lengthen your distance, doing an unpowered landing you adjust the length of your flight path to match available energy. Essentially this means, if you’re getting low, turn toward the runway, and if you seem high, turn away. At the very last moment when you are sure you won’t be short, you can add extra flaps or start a slip to bleed off excess energy. All pilots spend some time practicing this. It’s actually not that hard, in some ways easier than a powered landing. We don’t do it in normal practice because it’s very dangerous to have many dissimilar airplanes doing this at the same time, whereas normal powered approaches make dealing with traffic much safer.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why did the actual pictures of the earth show that the earth is round and not oblate spheroid? I think it is because almost half of the earth is covered by darkness so the camera cannot take a full view of the entire earth.
Answer: That’s certainly a real issue. But the actual reason? The Earth’s shape is very, very close to a sphere. The differences are not obvious to the eye. Wikipedia has a great visualisation of this, which I’m going to link because Quora will mess it up if I insert it directly: Are you really going to see the difference in a photo? Not without very carefully measuring, and knowing the exact distortion figures for the lens used. You could do that, but it’s not going to be apparent just looking at the image.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can you explain what wake vortices are in relation to jet engines?
Answer: They’re not about jet engines. All aircraft produce a wake of some sort. Anything with wings, propellers, or rotors produces tip vortex wakes. For a plane, this takes the form of a horizontal tornado-like vortex produced at each wing tip, and at the outer ends of the flaps if flaps are extended. Plus propeller wakes, which are the same thing coming from the tip of each prop blade, and thus form a helix trailing behind the engine. Jets don’t actually produce a wake vortex, just a jet blast, which doesn’t have much rotation at all (because that would be a waste of power, so the engine designers don’t let it happen). Wakes can be very dangerous; a heavy airplane’s wake can cause a complete loss of control for anything flying in to it.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can someone become an expert programmer or software developer without any prior experience or education in computer science?
Answer: Of course. Every expert was a beginner once. It takes a bunch of time, and you have to think about the opportunity cost and so forth. It may not be a wise decision, depending on your circumstances.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How long does it take for light from an exploding star to reach Earth? Can we predict the brightness of an exploding star if we were to see it immediately after its explosion?
Answer: How long depends on how far away it is, which could be anything from decades to billions of years. But the brighness of some kinds of supernova is very consistent, so if we see one and can observe it for long enough to determine what kind it was, we can often tell how far away it was too. In fact, that’s one of the standard ways to work out distances in the universe. Astronomers see a few thousand supernovae in distant galaxies every month, so many that the process of observing them is completely automated. The nearby ones that determine the brightness calibration, though, are quite rare.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can a DSLR camera be disassembled and reassembled safely? If so, what is the process for doing so?
Answer: It can. But… the process is basically “obtain a copy of the service manual, check what it requires for tools, obtain those, and do exactly what it says”. The first step is probably quite difficult, and the third may be impossible.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can a CNC machine be built from scratch without using a pre-existing model as a base? If not, what materials and resources would be needed to start building one from scratch?
Answer: Sure can. In fact, I’m considering doing exactly that. The easy way is to find a commercially produced kit of an open source design, for example one of the Openbuilds designs. Or, you can go find an open source design that you like, and source all the intems required for yourself. That’s quite a bit more work, and probably not cheaper, but doable. There will be a list or spreadsheet of all that stuff on the project website, usually called a BOM (for “Bill of Materials”). If you’re asking this question, you’re not up to designing one. Maybe one day, but for now don’t try that path. Right now I’m looking at the available designs and considering what I want to build. By the way, this answer applies equally to 3D printers, except that I’m not considering, I already built two.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for a person with no prior experience in building or flying aircraft to design and create their own airplane?
Answer: Like all these sorts of “no prior experience” questions… yes, but. The only way to be successful in doing something like that is to somehow get the benefit of the experience. So, you could study a lot in the library, buy components that already have the experience baked in, hire somebody to do parts of the design or build, take classes in construction techniques, maybe get an airplane mechanic license, take the time to go around aviation museums and the repair shops at airports and study what they do, and get a pilot license. Maybe do some simulator time and build some models as well. Likely, all of the above, and then some. So… yes, but it’s going to be a ton of work, and if you succeed you’ll have the experience. If you don’t succeed, you’ll probably learn a lot in the process. Just don’t try to fly something manned without getting a proper design review and learning to fly first… that’s a great way to die very quickly.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If we can fit billions of switches into one CPU as someone told me, is it because we are using atomic-size gates?
Answer: We can, and almost. The feature sizes in CPUs are a few hundred atoms across. Memory has smaller features.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it necessary to go through security again if you have connecting flights in different terminals of the same airport?
Answer: That depends on the airport. Some you do, some you don’t, some it can go either way depending on which terminals you are talking about.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is this practical? A boat with a jet engine that uses a very high torque output gearbox that compresses water and shoots it out for thrust.
Answer: Yes, it’s practical. Propellers are used more often, because they are more efficient. But a jetboat has two huge advantages: a prop strike is impossible, and with clever intake design, it’s also just about impossible to destroy the jet unit or the engine by ingesting gravel or sand. That means a jetboat can run in minimal water, in some cases where the water level is below the level of the gravel in a river bed (yes, really). Secondly, jetboats are also extremely maneuverable, so they have advantages for applications like search and rescue. It is quite possible for a twin-engine jetboat to move in any direction without turning, which is very useful when trying to come alongside another boat in poor conditions. The ability to beach the boat without much consequence is also really useful for SAR. And in racing… a jetsprint boat may not have that fast of a top speed, but it will accelerate nearly as hard as a top fuel drag car, and out-corner any race car, including F1.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What led to the replacement of Java with JavaScript on websites like Facebook and Google, which were originally built using Java?
Answer: They weren’t originally built using Java, at least not in the way you seem to be implying. Java itself had very little use in the browser, so little that it is now completely obsolete for that. Javascript, which is an entirely different language, was developed for use in browsers. Only later did it even become possible to use it for server applications. Now… Google (I can’t speak to Facebook) does use a fair bit of Java on the server side (Drive and Maps are both mostly in Java). Google also doesn’t really use very much Javascript in the backend, though I’m sure there is some.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: As a computer engineer what coding languages should I learn (name them please)?
Answer: Don’t worry about which languages matter when you are starting out. Instead, think of it this way: through your career you will more than likely use lots of languages. I’ve lost count. I know it’s more than 40, though the vast majority of my work has been in only six of those. So the trick is to learn how to learn languages quickly. You do this by learning lots of languages early on. But first, you have to learn programming, which is a language-independent skill. Unfortunately, you have to learn a whole stack of things simultaneously when you start out: programming itself, debugging, some language, and some set of tools that will let you use that language (an editor, maybe a build system, maybe a debugger, version control…) Your first language should probably be something relatively easy, as you have all that extra load to deal with. Easy languages, however, are not typically the really important languages, either important because they’re widely used in industry, or important because of what they teach you. Later, whatever your first language, you should spend a bit of time learning one from each major language family (procedural, functional, object oriented, dynamic, lazily evaluated, declarative, etc). That will make the ones you have to learn later much easier.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the minimum speed a jet must be going for it to be audible?
Answer: You’ve obviously never been outside near an airport. Zero. They’re really freaking loud at ground idle. As in, you can hear them kilometers away. In fact, even with just the APU running, they’re pretty loud, and that’s just the auxiliary generator that helps start the plane and provide power and air conditioning on the ground. People who work airside need hearing protection because jet APUs are so noisy.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for people to connect to your home wifi if they are in range, even if your network is hidden from view on the router?
Answer: Hiding the network name does precisely nothing useful. It only inconveniences you, so don’t even bother. It is still possible to tell the network is there and connect to it, if it does not use authentication. Use WPA2 at least, WPA3 if you can, and make sure your password remains known only to people you want connecting to the network. Or, set up enterprise authentication, and give usernames and passwords to people you want connecting; that way you can lock or remove their username when you have a reason to.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How many unique IPv4 addresses does each web server have access to?
Answer: There’s no answer to that question that makes sense. I mean… we can assume it’s not negative, but otherwise all bets are off. There may be only one. There may be one address shared by a great many servers. There may be many instances of that, each with slightly different server pools. Each server may have many addresses, some of which may be shared. Or indeed, a web server could be IPv6 only and have no IPv4 addresses at all. And if you mean… what client addresses can each server talk to? Ideally all of them, but of course it is never the case that the entire network is working correctly. And then there’s the exception, for backed servers that are never supposed to talk to a client directly.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How do I find a website’s IP address?
Answer: You can ask DNS. But… don’t assume a website has only one IP address, and don’t assume that there are not a number of websites at any particular address. Most large sites use content distribution networks, and they do a variety of complex things with IP addressing and HTTP that mean you can’t really assume anything about addresses. If you make a DNS request followed by an HTTP request from the same source, then the addresses you got from DNS will work for at least the lifetime specified in that response. You can’t assume more. Especially, the addresses will change, and the answers you get will depend on where you ask from and when, and possibly on which software you make the request with as well. In particular… you can’t put an address for a website into a firewall and expect it to either allow access reliably or deny access reliably. That just doesn’t work.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the reason for using one piece of wood for the neck and fingerboard of a guitar instead of multiple pieces? Can't they be glued together like other furniture items?
Answer: The neck is usually between one and three pieces, and the fingerboard is normally a separate part. So they are normally glued up. You have to be able to get the truss rod installed somehow, and that lives under the fretboard, so either you put a slot in from the back of the neck (really hard) or you make a separate neck and fretboard (relatively easy). Often the head starts out as a separate piece from the rest of the neck, and on acoustic guitars often part of the heel does as well. A joint in the middle of the neck is a really bad idea, though, it will make it very difficult to shape the part correctly. Many electric guitars have a scarf joint, as this dramatically reduces the size of the neck blank: The truss rod is routed out after doing this, and installed when the fretboard is glued on. There’s sometimes a cap or veneer on the headstock as well. However… sometimes a maker just wants to carve the whole neck in one go, and nothing really prevents that, especially if it’s a nylon string instrument that won’t have a truss rod.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How does the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) determine which port to use for a connection?
Answer: That’s left to protocols that use TCP, and/or the implementation. For example, HTTP usually uses port 80 for servers, but clients can use any port their OS sees fit to use. HTTP also allows non-standard ports in a URL; http://example.com:8080/ for example. Clients for most protocols will simply open a connection to a known server IP and port number, and let the operating system pick any suitable outgoing port; the only constraint is that it cannot already be in use to the same destination IP and port number; obviously if that were allowed, it would be impossible to tell two connections apart.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Are there any plans available for building a replica of Brian May's "Red Special" guitar?
Answer: Of course there are. Have you built a guitar before? If not, I really recommend not starting with a Red Special, that’s a very difficult design to do well. Not to mention expensive, so getting it wrong is a major setback.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to build a small fusion power generator for personal use? How feasible is it? Will it be achievable in our lifetime?
Answer: Small and fusion power are not compatible, sorry. The thing is… any reasonable fusion power cycle produces some radiation along with the power, and you need a bit of room to render that safe. A minimum of about a two meter thick layer of the right materials around the outside of your reactor, in fact. Or five meters, if the right materials are too expensive. So… you almost certainly don’t have space for the reactor’s shielding, pretty much no matter how big the reactor itself ends up being. And of course, a few hundred cubic meters of any solid ends up costing rather a lot… Now… all the current candidates for practical reactor designs are themselves pretty big and will be rather expensive as well, and of course the bigger the reactor the more stuff you need to shield it. So… nope, not feasible. Not because of lack of technology, but because it’s too bulky for nearly any individual. Not that big compared to a coal or fission power plant, but still too big for residential use.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can airline pilots sleep during long flights and still be able to wake up and land safely at any time? Is this possible because of auto-pilot modes?
Answer: Really long flights have enough crew that nobody has to exceed their duty time limits, and there’s somewhere to rest for the off-duty crew. But the aircraft is not automated enough that there is ever a time that there isn’t a full crew at least monitoring what is going on. That’s necessary for safety. So… if a crew member has been asleep and it’s time for them to go back on duty, it’s not to do with autopilot, it’s because someone will wake them up if they don’t do it themselves. This applies to cabin crew just as much as to pilots, by the way.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How do you start a jet engine on a commercial airplane? Is the procedure different from starting a piston aircraft?
Answer: The procedure is different for every different airplane, whether piston, turboprop, jet, or electric. One of the things you have to do when getting checked out for a different plane is learn all its procedures, including how to start and shut down correctly without breaking anything (or worse).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do violins and guitars use the same chord progressions?
Answer: Chord progressions are music theory. That should be a hint: theory is about music in general. All instruments, and vocals too, use the same theory, although we should remember that different cultures have traditions that don’t work in necessarily compatible ways. However… violins and guitars both originate in Europe, from the same musical tradition near enough. So yes, they use the same chord progressions. It is, however, not possible to use them in exactly the same way, because guitar chord voicings aren’t necessarily reachable on violin, nor vice versa.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do airliners typically use only one type of engine, either turbofan or turboprop? If so, why don't they use both types simultaneously?
Answer: They’re trying to use both simultaneously, sort of, using something called an unducted fan. The problem with those is that they’re way too loud, though the engine manufacturers keep trying to solve that. There’s a good reason not to combine jets and turboprops. If you do that (there have been a couple of military aircraft that did), you lose all the advantages of the jets, and just end up with a really inefficient turboprop. You use turboprops for applications where climb and descent rate, and/or runway length constraints, are important. Turboprops have far more thrust at low speeds, so they allow use of shorter runways and steeper climbs. Turboprops also make incredibly effective air brakes, allowing very short landing distances and descents that are ridiculously steep (some turboprop aircraft can safely control their speed while flying straight down). The disadvantage of a turboprop is that it isn’t as fast. Seldom more than Mach 0.75, where jets often cruise between Mach 0.85 and Mach 0.9. You use jets where high speed cruise economy matters most. Or if you want to fly supersonic, because a turboprop can’t do that. This is why short-haul airliners are often turboprops, and why all the longest range airliners are jets; if you can get to cruise altitude sooner and descend faster on a short trip, you might be able to get there sooner even if the cruise speed is a bit lower. And you get to use smaller airports. So… if you fit any turboprop engines, you get the turboprop speed limit. Adding jets to that aircraft won’t make it faster, but it will dilute the turboprop advantages, in which case if you need more engines they may as well be the same turboprops. That also simplifies maintenance. Unducted fans are the best of both worlds, with most of the turboprop advantages and without the speed limit; they’d still have to stay below the speed of sound, but would keep up with the jets. Unfortunately, like I said, they’re impossibly noisy at the moment (and it’s not a nice sound either, it’s a howl with a really harsh edge to it).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is replacing spark plugs beneficial for older cars, or is it only necessary for newer vehicles with higher compression ratios and smaller spark plug gaps?
Answer: Old cars needed their plugs changed frequently. Often the service manual suggested every second service, or as required in between. Newer cars almost never need plugs changed. They can go hundreds of thousands of km with the factory plugs still in place. That’s because the plugs are far more durable, and the ignition systems much more gentle on the plug. The usual reason for needing to change plugs is actually a coil pack failure damaging the plug, and most times a failing coil doesn’t do that. Coils fail way more often than plugs. Even though the plugs are much more expensive, you end up not spending nearly as much on ignition maintenance because you just don’t have to touch them.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How long would it take to reach low-earth orbit from the surface of the Earth using a plane with current technology that can accommodate passengers and their luggage comfortably?
Answer: Infinitely long. You would never get there. Planes can’t do that. If, however, you fitted out a SpaceX Starship with an appropriate interior and life support system… about eight minutes. It would then take a couple of hours to maneuver to dock with another orbiting vehicle. It could also point-to-point between two spots on the Earth in about 30 to 45 minutes, depending on where exactly they were.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to build rockets that can break out of our solar system's gravity and travel into Interstellar space? Are there any limitations in our current understanding of physics that would prevent this?
Answer: Not only possible, we’ve done it. The Voyager probes were launched in 1977, and by now both are in interstellar space, Voyager 1 since 2012 and Voyager 2 since 2018.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If the universe only consisted of stars and no planets like ours, would we be aware of this?
Answer: Yes, we would, and it does not. The reason being, we have an ever-growing catalogue of confirmed planets orbiting other stars. One place you can see that list is As of right now, there are 5666 planets in the database. And remember… that’s confirmed planets.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What are the rules for bringing prescription medication on an airplane? What are the consequences if law enforcement finds it during a pat down or search?
Answer: Domestic flights in every country I’m aware of: No problem, just follow the liquids rules if any of it is liquid, though there are exceptions for medicines. Look them up. International travel: Make sure your essential prescriptions are legal in all the countries you will be passing through before you buy the tickets. Make sure you have documentation that the medicine was actually prescribed (many countries have pharmacies put stickers on the packaging, so don’t repack your medicines unless you have copies of the actual prescriptions). Obviously, consider if the prescription is essential if it’s not legal where you are going. The common issues are Marijuana derivatives in many countries, Modafinil and ADHD medications going to Japan. Look up and understand the rules for the particular country. Often it is legal for a visitor to bring in and use prescriptions that would be illegal to prescribe in that country. But remember: prescription medications are a specific category in air transport and customs regulations all over the world, and are mostly allowed. You just have to show that yes, they really are prescription, and make sure to respect the exceptions.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What are the reasons for major carmakers not transitioning directly to fully electric cars instead of hybrid ones?
Answer: Even if they wanted to do it overnight, which many don’t, they simply can’t. You need time and money to switch a car factory over to producing an even slightly different model. When the design is radically different, which it is for an EV, that takes a lot more time and money. Hybrids are much easier to fit in to the production process. And of course… EVs need a radically different kind of battery, which you have to build, and it takes huge amounts of money and time to set up that process. So, they’re not there yet because there hasn’t been enough time.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If I play an electric bass guitar with only headphones in a condo, will neighbors still hear it through the walls?
Answer: Only if your walls are ridiculously thin. Most of the sound an electric bass makes acoustically is string clatter, and other quite high-pitched sounds. It isn’t particularly loud and doesn’t travel much. Let’s put it this way: if that’s enough to annoy your neighbours, anything would, and they’re unreasonable.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If gravity is a warping of space-time, why is it that we see no distortions in our visual field?
Answer: It’s a matter of how much gravity bends light. Which isn’t much at all. Light travels very, very fast, and though it falls just like anything else, that doesn’t end up bending its path by much of an angle. Slower moving things, like you and I, or planets, have their paths bent much more. Which is why you don’t see light bending due to gravity in any ordinary everyday context; the distances are too small and light is much too fast. However, on an astronomical scale… we do see those distortions. Stars look to be in slightly different places when their light passes close to the Sun, Mercury and Jupiter’s moons have slightly different orbits because of the bending of time as they orbit, and on a really large scale we see gravitational lenses like this: Capturing an image like that requires a professional observatory or a space telescope, it is way beyond difficult. That light had to travel almost half way across the observable universe, and it required the gravity of a very large galaxy (the orange one in the center) to create the lens.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to install a floating bridge on any type of guitar? If not, which types of guitars cannot have a floating bridge installed later on?
Answer: My view, having built a few guitars with both hardtail and floating bridges, is that it is never worthwhile installing a floating bridge after the fact. The operations to make the bridge cavity happen right near the beginning of making the guitar body, and are really easy then. After the body is finished, you no longer have any of the reference marks or surfaces you need to make that cavity. Changing from one hardtail bridge to another, or from one floating bridge to another of the same general type, sure, you can do that. But use a body that was made for the basic family of bridge, don’t try to switch them. And of course… it is, just barely, possible to build an acoustic with a floating bridge, but the whole instrument has to be designed for that from the very beginning, and a retrofit is just impossible.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can a computer be built in a small case like an Apple Mac Mini?
Answer: A Mac Mini is a computer. Facetious answer over… I suspect you mean a Windows computer. Well… I suggest you look up something called an Intel NUC. The category is called a “Mini PC”, there are a few more than just the Intel machines.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a way to determine if a computer has built-in WiFi without physically opening it?
Answer: You can boot it up and see if the OS shows you a WiFi device. Or, if it’s a prebuilt machine (laptop, or name-brand desktop) you can find the FCC ID sticker that will be on it somewhere, then look it up in the FCC database to see what it was certified as. EU certifications can be used the same way (so can Chinese, but you need to read Chinese to use that one). If you can’t do either, and there are no antenna connectors or antennas visible, then no, you’ll have to take a look.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What applications or industries use the Linux/Unix operating system? I know Linux has a loyal personal use fan base, but am curious where it is used commercially.
Answer: Everywhere. Every cloud provider, almost all websites, a huge number of embedded systems (many printers, for example), most routers (at any scale, from home routers to data centers), car entertainment systems. Most large companies have some Linux somewhere. Android is Linux too, as are most TV’s operating systems. The thing is, Linux is used a lot in systems where it’s not clear from the outside there even is an OS there, and in systems which no end user interacts with directly. But just because you don’t see it doesn’t mean it’s not there.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do all electric and acoustic guitars have a truss rod for adjusting the curvature of the neck, or is it only found in certain models such as Fender Stratocasters?
Answer: Almost all electric guitars have truss rods… I’m sure there are a few exceptions, but I couldn’t point you at one. Few nylon-string guitars have truss rods. The string tension is low enough that it’s not necessary for structural reasons, though high end instruments may still fit one for adjustability. More steel-string acoustic guitars have truss rods, because the string tension is higher. It’s still not all, though personally I wouldn’t buy a steel string without one, that’s just asking for trouble. Electric basses almost universally have truss rods. The adjustability is necessary with such a long, skinny neck (though the string tension is actually quite low).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Effects pedals for bass guitar - which are essential, and which are superfluous?
Answer: If your amp doesn’t have them, bass-voiced tone controls (also called EQ), and a compressor are essential. An overdrive with a clean/drive blend is not essential exactly, but commonly used. There are bass preamp pedals that do everything necessary in one unit, and let you use a clean PA-style amp. This is actually cheaper and often better than an actual bass amp. A strobe tuner, like a TC Polytune, is a really useful thing to have. That’s it. Bass doesn’t much need effects.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it common for fingers on the fretting hand to experience pain after playing guitar for an hour or two?
Answer: Yes. If it starts to hurt… stop. Ideally, stop just before that, when you can feel your hands are tired but before they actually hurt. You need to build up fitness, and playing till it hurts slows that down. After a few months, you’ll find you can play longer before it becomes a problem.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What causes the sonic boom to be heard from an aircraft's cockpit and not from any other part of the aircraft?
Answer: That doesn’t happen. Sonic booms can not be heard anywhere on board the aircraft that creates them. Other aircraft, or on the ground, sure. But on board a supersonic aircraft… things get somewhat quieter as the aircraft starts to outrun the noise it is creating itself. No boom.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why are we still making batteries instead of using clean hydrogen fuel cells, despite having access to green energy?
Answer: Hydrogen absolutely sucks as a fuel for ground vehicles. It’s dangerous to work with, requires crazy materials to keep it contained reliably, fuel cells need a lot of maintenance. All of that translates into a rather expensive vehicle. Batteries are relatively nice. Not so many strange materials, much less maintenance, less danger. On top of that, if you generate a certain amount of electricity, you’ll lose about 45% of it going through hydrogen production, the distribution chain for that hydrogen, then using it in the fuel cell. Whereas, if you feed it across the power grid to charge batteries, you only lose something between 8% and 15%, depending on how good the grid is and how far it has to go. Generation is not free, so hydrogen ends up being about 3x as expensive, all things considered. Batteries are cheaper and better than fuel cells, so where possible, that’s what we use.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why don't electric vehicles have manual transmissions or stick shifts like gasoline vehicles? Would it improve their performance and efficiency?
Answer: They don’t usually have selectable gear ratios at all. Think of it like a manual that’s been welded into second gear (that’s usually roughly what the ratio is) and the clutch pedal removed. So the “shifter” on the dash is actually just a switch that tells the motor controller what mode to use. Select reverse, it runs backwards. Select neutral, it just turns the motor off. Select park, it applies some sort of transmission brake (like an automatic in park). The reason for this is pretty simple: combustion engines only work well over a fairly narrow range of RPM, but the speed range you want for the vehicle is much wider. The solution is to change gear ratios. But electric motors work well over a very wide range of RPM, wide enough that you don’t need to select gear ratios. So it makes sense to remove all the parts that allow that, so you have a much simpler transmission (often just a single pair of reduction gears, or even a final drive built with the right ratio driven directly from the motor). Some electric motors can have their effective speed range changed electronically (by changing what combinations of coils each phase of the motor uses). This is used in electric trains, and could be used in electric road vehicles too, though I don’t know of it having been done (if it has, it would probably be trucks and buses rather than cars). That would give fully electronic gear selection with no moving parts, which would be way better than any selectable mechanical transmission.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why does your ISP handle your internet connection instead of your computer being directly connected to the rest of the world's internet?
Answer: Connecting to the Internet is actually fairly complicated, and unless you’re in to extremely expensive, complex, and time consuming hobbies, not something you want to do yourself. One of the main reasons it’s complicated is that it’s actually fairly easy to break the global Internet. All of it, that is. So, the penalties for getting it wrong are pretty steep… including immediate disconnection, and an onerous process of proving you know what you are doing in order to get reconnected. Effectively, you’re outsourcing a lot of time and effort, plus a rather large liability, in exchange for a little bit of money. It’s only as cheap as it is because the ISP has economies of scale; the connecting to the Internet part is not really that much more complicated for thousands or millions of users as it is for one. Of course, not all of the business scales like that.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What happens to an electric guitar that is left out on display with tuned strings for an extended period of time?
Answer: Nothing much. It will of course get dusty. The strings might rust. The finish may fade if there’s significant UV light in the room. But, guitars are meant to have string tension on; it does more damage to take the strings down in tension or completely off than it does just to leave them there. In fact, personally I think it’s better to tune it every now and again, even if it isn’t otherwise being played.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: I have a hard-tail Charvel that I need a tremolo system installed into. Many guitar techs have refused and some have told me to outright purchase a new guitar body. Is wood routing really that difficult and expensive?
Answer: The problem is this: the best time to start installing a tremelo is right when you start making the body, as part of the initial operations where you make the neck pocket, pickup cavities, and electronics cavities. This is before any body carving and before even making the outline of the body, while it is still just a slab of wood. It’s quick and easy, done at that point. Tape on some templates, route them out, repeat a few times, done. Maybe 30 minutes to do the whole job. Doing it afterward is really, really hard, because the finishing operations have destroyed all the reference marks and reference surfaces you need to do it the easy way. So now you have to spend several hours making very careful measurements, then make some jigs that you will probably only use this one time, then very carefully route without messing up the rest of the finish. You are much better off to buy a guitar with a tremelo and keep your hardtail how it is.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the reason for the curved shape of a plane's wings? Why can't they be completely flat?
Answer: You can build a plane with flat wings, and it will fly, given enough power. However… other than model airplanes, we don’t do that, because flat plate wings are not the best for efficiency. In fact, they’re pretty awful. Even the Wright Flyer had carefully shaped wings, because the engine they could build, despite having the best power to weight ratio of any engine up to that date, did not have enough power to fly flat plate wings. Any airplane since has had some kind of airfoil because the designers know you can do better than flat plates for power requirements, fuel efficiency, altitude, handling, and glide distance, all of which matter one way or another. There are thousands of published airfoil sections, and textbooks on how to make new ones, so if you are designing a plane you have plenty of options to go for an airfoil that will do the best for your requirements.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Will there be a faster Internet connection than 5G in the future? Or will 5G remain the fastest option?
Answer: 5G is nowhere near the fastest option even now. There are many kinds of fiber connection that are much faster than 5G, and some of those are even available as residential or small business connections in some parts of the world. When you get up to large business connections… some of them are hundreds or even thousands of times as fast as a 5G connection. After all… the 5G system has to connect the base stations to the Internet somehow. If you have the money, you can use that technology too. One of the issues with 5G is that it is next to impossible to predict how fast it will actually be from minute to minute, whereas fiber systems are very consistent.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to get burned by the exhaust of a running helicopter engine, even though it is not as hot as jet engines on airplanes?
Answer: Oh yes. It may not be as hot as jet exhaust… but it’s still very, very hot. If it’s a turbine helicopter, the exhaust temperature at idle will be very similar to the exhaust temperature of an idling jet, about 500 C. The jet may get much hotter at high power settings, the helicopter not so much. If it’s a piston helicopter, well, it’s much like a car engine, and the exhaust pipe will still be hot enough to burn, even if the gas doesn’t have the heat capacity to do so.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a faster alternative to Ethernet that can currently replace it in terms of technology and the TCP/IP stack?
Answer: Ethernet itself keeps getting faster variants. You’re probably familiar with gigabit ethernet, it’s everywhere. 10 and 100 megabit ethernet are kind of historical at this point. You might be aware that there is 10 gigabit ethernet. But there’s also 2.5, 5, 25, 40, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, and (soon) 1600 gigabit ethernet. What is really going on is that people keep inventing new physical layers, and putting the ethernet protocol on top of them because that’s the easiest way to get useful applications running.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a reason why airliners do not have a dump valve for excess fuel in their wings? Would it be possible for them to land without burning off the excess fuel?
Answer: Before you ask why not, ask if. Because many airliners and other large planes (not all) actually can dump fuel if the situation demands. It’s an emergency feature, to deal with those airplanes where the maximum takeoff weight is far higher than the maximum landing weight… which means that if you have an issue shortly after takeoff, you can not land immediately. But if you can dump fuel, you can land a lot sooner than if you had to burn it. That of course presumes that the issue has not also caused problems with the dump system, which has happened. Sometimes the designers conclude that a dump system isn’t worth the weight or complexity, and don’t fit one. This is usually for somewhat smaller aircraft, which will never have tens or hundreds of tons of extra fuel.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can a transport layer protocol be created that has better performance than TCP and UDP?
Answer: Sure. You do have to define ‘performance’ and ‘better’, though, because there are multiple possible definitions and the differences matter. QUIC (as used in HTTP/3) may be the leading contender for that better protocol. But SCTP, DTLS, LEDBAT, and a few others, might also be better, depending on what exactly you want. If you are working in this field, you also need to be aware that QUIC, TCP, and SCTP are all moving targets; they get frequent upgrades too. So what it means to be “better than TCP” may not remain the same from month to month.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: The EV was invented before the gas car. The gas car killed off the EV market by the free market. Why do some people think all people will switch to EV this time?
Answer: In the meantime, we have invented three crucial technologies that make all the difference. One, better batteries. All they had then was lead-acid, which… well, are made of lead. They’re really heavy for their energy capacity. Modern batteries are vastly better. Two, MOSFETs. All they had was manual switches (which means no throttle control) or resistive control (meaning really horrible efficiency). MOSFETs enable switch-mode electronic speed control, which gives an efficiency around 90% and perfect throttle control. MOSFETs also allow much more efficient and faster chargers. Three, microcontrollers. These allow us to control those MOSFETs accurately, and keep track of the battery charge. Without those, you had no way to know how much range remained in your batteries, other than the performance starting to drop. This is, admittedly, much worse with modern batteries, which tend to perform pretty much the same till the charge gets really low and then suddenly die.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is stopping electric car makers from making electric cars that are self-charging from the motion they produce in the act of driving?
Answer: Physics. What you are suggesting is, quite simply, not possible. It’s one of the laws of thermodynamics, and there are no exceptions. But… there are a couple of ways it is sort of possible, and EVs do use those. A car has to have a way to slow down and stop. Combustion vehicles use mechanical brakes to do that, which convert the motion of the vehicle into heat. EVs do have mechanical brakes, but they’re mostly a safety sytem. What an EV can do is use the motors as generators, and use the resulting power to charge the battery. That is, in a sense, self-charging. But you get back less energy than you put in to get the vehicle moving in the first place, so it’s only an improvement in efficiency. If you start out at the top of a hill, you can get to the bottom with more battery charge… that is some of the energy it took to get the vehicle to the top of the hill in the first place. Now, if the EV in question is a mining truck, and the mine is at the top of a hill, and the place where the ore and spoil is going is at the bottom, then you can use this to charge the truck… because you’re moving a lot of heavy stuff down the hill, and going back up empty. So you can take the energy difference between ore up a hill and ore down a hill, and feed some of it into the truck’s batteries. But aside from that sort of special situation, no, you can’t really do this.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it true that all devices connected to a Wi-Fi network have the same IP address and MAC address?
Answer: No. They all have different IP addresses, though on the outside of the network they often share an IPv4 address. They also all have different MAC addresses.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do multiple people sharing an Internet connection each have their own unique external IP address?
Answer: Most of the time, in IPv4, no. Almost always in IPv6, yes. IPv4 does not have enough addresses to number the current Internet, so addresses are shared, by use of NAT (network address translation, which comes in several varieties). In fact, it’s fairly common that external IP addresses will be shared between multiple connections (so-called Carrier Grade NAT, for example). More than likely you have never used a network that didn’t share IPv4 addresses. IPv6 has plenty of addresses, so while NAT is possible, it’s very rare. Most devices on an IPv6 network will have many addresses, in fact. So… it depends.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do programmers do anything with graph theory?
Answer: Programmers do a whole lot with graph theory. Any non-trivial datastructure can be represented as a graph, so there’s one huge field for a start. File systems are graphs. Networks are graphs. There’s this little thing called the Internet… which is a directed multigraph in nearly any sensible representation within software. Compiler optimisers are often written explicitly in terms of manipulating abstract syntax trees or dataflow diagrams… both of which are kinds of graph. Depending on what kind of programming you end up doing, it may not be a daily thing to use graph theory explicitly, but it is one of the fields you need to know the basics of and where to go looking for the advanced techniques, for those occasions when you need it; it will happen from time to time.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: When HTTP is used over TCP, which happens first, HTTP’s GET request or TCP’s 3-way handshake?
Answer: It depends. If it’s HTTP/3, there isn’t going to be a TCP handshake, and the GET request can be carried in the QUIC handshake along with everything else. If you have a fast reconnect token, the handshake doesn’t happen, you just get a resumed session with an immediate response. If it’s HTTP/2 or below, and you have a valid TCP fast reconnect token, there isn’t going to be a TCP handshake, and the GET request is in the first packet. If it’s HTTP/2 or below and you have an invalid token or no token at all, the GET request comes after the handshake; if the token was invalid, the request will likely have to be retransmitted.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Could one run an internet without TCP/IP, but with UNIX domain sockets?
Answer: No. UNIX domain sockets are local to the machine. They don’t go anywhere. You can build protocols that run on whatever media your machine has using raw sockets. However, you’re asking about an internet. There can be only one, at lest in the long term. Why is this? One of the first things anyone does with a new network is connect it to the capital-I Internet, which makes it part of the Internet not a separate entity.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can you legally take open source code, modify it, and sell the software as closed source?
Answer: Read the license. Sometimes you can, sometimes you can’t. BSD licensed code, yes, you can do that. Apple’s operating systems are derived from a lot of BSD licensed code (plus a vast amount of their own work). The same is true of some of Windows.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can someone become a machine learning engineer without any prior experience in programming languages such as Python and Java?
Answer: Everyone has to start somwhere. Machine learning isn’t actually that complex as a programming problem, it’s more of a mathematical problem. Obviously if you go in to it without the math or programming, it’s going to take longer to learn everything required. It is just a big pile of stuff to learn. Knowing where you already know, and know what is in the pile, you can work through it. But it is much, much easier if you can find a course where someone has already worked through that and can present it in a reasonable order… and if you don’t have the prerequisites for the course, go find courses for them.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to make money from programming without knowing any coding? Would the end product be flawed due to the lack of coding knowledge?
Answer: If you try a solo project and know nothing about programming, there will not be an end product. Or else, by the end, you will know rather a lot about programming. More than likely the product will be seriously flawed, but if you’re a really detail-oriented person, it may just take a really long time to get there. Now, if you are a member of a large team, with the right sort of product there may be roles that don’t require programming.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How long does it typically take for someone with advanced guitar skills to learn how to build one from scratch for personal use?
Answer: Building an instrument has absolutely nothing to do with playing it. It’s entirely possible to build an instrument that you cannot play at all. What matters much more are your woodworking, metalworking, and to some extent electronics skills. That said… there are various places around the world that teach guitar building, and you can build a guitar in a 3 month full time course (using their equipment). That seems like a realistic estimate of how much time it takes. Of course, three months full time is not long enough to be an expert at all, but you could realistically have a playable instrument in the equivalent time. I will point out… the tools and materials to build a guitar cost a lot more than most factory built guitars. This isn’t a way to save money, unless you would have to go to a custom shop to get exactly what you want. Even then, a custom shop instrument will be better than your first few instruments. If you already have a well equipped woodworking shop, then of course it becomes a lot cheaper, and you probably have far more of the skills as well.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: When you look into the night sky, are you seeing other galaxies, or just our own Milky Way stars?
Answer: Most of what you see is in the Milky Way, especially if you’re in the Northern Hemisphere. Not all of it is stars, there’s a bit of light reflected off dust, and a bit of emission from interstellar gas. And of course, some of the other planets in our own solar system are visible without a telescope. But, there are nine other galaxies visible to the naked eye. Two of them, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, are easily visible from the Southern Hemisphere (they’re also close enough that you can see a few individual stars in them). In the northern sky, the Andromeda galaxy can be seen fairly easily. The other six are difficult, you need to know exactly where to look and have basically perfect conditions.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How much money would you save by filling your car with airplane jet fuel instead of regular gasoline? Why is it not possible to purchase jet fuel from a nearby airport for personal use?
Answer: Jet fuel is kerosene, so it doesn’t work in gasoline cars; it might run briefly, but it will produce lots of smoke and poison some of the engine’s sensors. Jet fuel does work in diesel cars, although you need to add a bit of ordinary diesel to each tank to protect the fuel pump and injectors (because diesel is a much better lubricant than kerosene). Whether it is legal to use aviation fuel for non-aviation uses depends on your local law. Often there’s a tax problem that makes it illegal to do so. But if it’s legal, you can very likely get some. Aircraft operators get their fuel by setting up an account with one of the fuel companies, who supply a swipe card that will activate the pumps on an airfield. You would also have to get an aviation security clearance and an airfield driving license (or a pilot license) to make it legal to drive to the pumps. At bigger airports, the fuel supplier could probably drive a fuel truck out of the secure area and deliver it that way. To your question about price: Jet fuel is slightly more expensive than road diesel, so you wouldn’t save money. Except, occasionally you can get tank drainings from maintenance facilities for free (since they’re not allowed to reload them into an aircraft, they would otherwise have to pay to dispose of it). You’d have to know someone to get fuel from that source though.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for a small planet to exist outside of our solar system in another Galaxy?
Answer: We now know of so many planets outside our solar system (about 5600) that we can be certain that nearly all stars have planets. That includes stars in other galaxies. As of right now there are no confirmed discoveries of extragalactic planets, though there are two candidate discoveries that have not yet been refuted. So: it’s more than possible, it’s certain that planets in other galaxies exist.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for a car's rear wheels to lock up without the front ones doing so as well? If not, how does this work mechanically?
Answer: Each wheel can lock up independent of all the others. So, yes, the rear end can lock up without the front end even getting close to a lockup. This is common with unloaded trucks and vans, as the weight over the rear end is insufficient to provide enough traction for the full power of the bakes. Some cheaper designs don’t include the balance valve that applies just enough rear brakes to do the job. It is also possible to lock the front wheels without locking the rear, though it doesn’t happen often. ABS, of course, solves this problem by not allowing the wheels to stay locked (though it might introduce more issues, especially on snow and ice).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the maximum speed one can travel in space without experiencing relativistic effects? Is there a limit before reaching the destination and returning?
Answer: There isn’t such a limit. Relativity applies all the time. Yes, even now as you read this, you are in Earth’s gravitational field, so time runs a bit slower for you than it does out in interstellar space. However… mostly they’re so small it takes precision instruments to measure them (the GPS in your phone does, for example). If you’re going to travel in space, what matters is how fast you go relative to the speed of light… and the speed of light is really, really fast. Therefore, interplanetary travel won’t create any appreciable relativistic effects, you’re not going fast enough. Yes, they would be easy enough to measure, but not enough to matter. Any reasonable way to achieve interstellar travel, though, is very likely to involve large relativistic effects.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: My friend bought us plane tickets for our vacation saying we were going to Australia but in reality we wound up in Austria. What should I do?
Answer: Groan at the joke and have fun in Austria. Both countries have great beer and fun stuff to do, what’s the problem? It’s a vacation after all.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to bring prescription medication onto a plane without declaring them in advance?
Answer: Nobody cares what you bring on to a plane, within the weight limit, unless it is one of two things: Prescription medicines are neither, or else exempt in some cases. However… When you get to your destination, if you have crossed an international border… then your destination may care what you take off the plane with you. Don’t try to bring items that are illegal, which may include prescription medication even if you have a valid prescription, into another country. This implies that if you are travelling internationally, you do need to look up if your prescriptions are legal in every country you will visit. Japan in particular has some very strict rules, but in general you should always check.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a type of plane that can take off vertically like a helicopter but fly like a regular airplane without using VTOL technology?
Answer: If an aircraft can do that… it is by definition VTOL. VTOL stands for “vertical takeoff and landing”. There are several ways of doing it, but they’re all VTOL.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is Cerenkov radiation only present in water or air, or can it occur in other mediums as well? How does it occur in these mediums if nothing can travel faster than light?
Answer: Nothing can travel faster than light travels in a vacuum. However… light itself travels slower than that in any material that isn’t a vacuum, sometimes rather a lot slower. Other particles can sometimes travel in that material faster than light will. If so, and the material doesn’t just absorb light, you get Cerenkov radiation. So… Cerenkov radiation can occur in any transparent material. Water, air, glass, gemstones (especially sapphire and diamond), plastics, and more.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to connect a router through Wi-Fi or does it only work with a wired connection (Ethernet)?
Answer: Possible? With the right kind of router, yes. Not all routers can do this, and certainly most home gateways you would get from an ISP can’t. “WiFi Mesh” systems effectively do this, kind of. A good idea? Well, not usually, but there are times it can make sense. Ubiquiti, as an easily remembered example, make a whole range of different routers that can do this kind of thing.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How can I get my Starlink cable to pass through through my electrical pipes in my home?
Answer: Those pipes are called conduit. Never put data cable in the same conduit as power. Never ever. It’s dangerous, because the data cable is not rated for mains. So… just don’t do that, or if you must have conduit put in some new conduit, sized to fit.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it more efficient and powerful to use jet engines in cars instead of petrol engines? Why are jet engines not commonly used in cars? Would it make sense to have jet engines on all wheels instead of just one?
Answer: No, turbine engines are awful for cars. Turbines are really efficient at very large sizes, in the tens of megawatts. At small sizes… and a car would be very small… the efficiency is terrible. Even the smallest aviation turbines are really too small to be efficient, but they’re used because they make up for that with really light weight and extreme reliability. About the smallest ground vehicle where a turbine engine makes sense is a locomotive, because that can use enough power to make some sense. So… don’t want a car with a fuel consumption measured in gallons per mile? Don’t use a turbine. Turbo-diesel engines are as efficient as a big turbine, but work at car sizes. This is kind of academic anyway, as the future belongs to electric vehicles… which can of course charge from a turbine power plant, which can be way more efficient than any other combustion engine of any sort, precisely because you can make it enormous.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why is maple not suitable for making electric bass bodies, but is suitable for guitars?
Answer: Maple isn’t ordinarily used for bodies even on guitars, for one simple reason: it’s very dense wood, and too heavy. Flamed and spalted maple are sometimes used as caps or veneers on bodies, because they look good, and a thin layer doesn’t weigh that much. Maple is an excellent option for making necks, though. But you could do a solid maple bass. It would work. It would just weigh a lot.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why don't aircraft use the jet stream in the atmosphere to fly faster or save energy?
Answer: Before you ask why not, ask if. They do, any time it’s possible. There are companies that specialise in constructing flight plans that make the absolute most of the current weather situation, using jet streams and whatever else might be going on. Airlines pay them for those flight plans when they need to get a flight somewhere in the minimum possible time. Some airlines do a lot of that work in-house, especially those that have many intercontinental routes (because obviously, the longer the flight, the more difference this makes). There are even some routes that are only possible because each flight has a team of people at the airline continuously working on weather optimisation, and communicating the results to the flight crew in real time.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What technologies are used by Google and Microsoft for their backend systems? Is Java still the primary server-side language for both companies?
Answer: Java was never the primary server-side language at Google (that’s C++), though Google does have quite a lot of Java code. I would be highly surprised if Java were particularly important at Microsoft either.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is there a programming language that uses English as its syntax? Why is it not widely used?
Answer: There might be, but there’s a good reason we use specialist languages for programming. The syntax of natural languages is much too ambiguous. Since you need a degree of precision that natural languages just don’t have, you’re immediately in to formal languages, and a different kind of syntax. The same sort of reason lies behind the use of mathematical and musical notation (not to mention many other kinds of notation that are more specialist and less well known).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do any known planets have moons that orbit the barycenter of their planetary systems instead of orbiting their parent planet directly?
Answer: All orbiting objects orbit around the barycenter of the system, to a very good first approximation. No exceptions. What’s unusual is if the barycenter is outside the surface of the most massive object. But all that requires is that two objects be close enough in mass. So, the barycenter of the solar system is usually outside the surface of the sun, because Jupiter and Saturn are so massive.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What happens to the dead core of a Super Nova, and have we found any dead Super Nova cores?
Answer: Depending on what sort of supernova and what the mass of the original star was, you get a black hole, a neutron star, or nothing but a cloud of gas. We have seen many, many examples of all of those. Outside our own galaxy, we observe around 20,000 supernovae every year, and we can easily tell which sort of remnant was left. Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why are we not going to the moon since we went last?
Answer: It’s astonishingly expensive to do that, and nobody could justify spending all that money. Really. It’s that simple.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why do they always show the planets perfectly round are they? Neil Tyson DeGrasse said that the Earth was pear-shaped what's up with that who's right who's wrong what the hell is going on?
Answer: What’s going on is that they’re almost, but not quite, perfectly round. The difference takes careful measurement to detect in most cases, it’s too small to see without instruments. One exception is Saturn; it spins fast enough that it’s visibly slightly squashed: Planets with a solid surface have more complicated shapes, but if they rotate reasonably quickly there’s always a little bit of that squash, even if it is too small to see. And yes, the Earth is a little bit pear-shaped. But the difference between the shape of the Earth and a perfect sphere is very small compared to the size of the Earth, and so it looks like a sphere until you start measuring. Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why do people so often assume cars are the only use of hydrogen? Surely the importance of it is that it is the only way we know of that is capable of storing enough energy to run our civilisation on renewables energy. Cars are a tiny part of that.
Answer: Hydrogen as energy storage is a terrible, terrible idea, with perhaps one exception: aircraft. But even for aircraft, there are probably better options (synthetic hydrocarbons or methanol, for example). Green hydrogen is still important, because it’s impossible to replace in the chemical industry, and we do need sustainable ways of making it. But for energy, it’s a losing proposition, because you lose so much energy in the process, and because it’s so expensive to store and transport. Not to mention dangerous.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: I think I need glasses, the lights look like stars at night and I also see double sometimes on bright text. Should I get my eyes tested?
Answer: Yes, you should. It might cost something, but it could well be a massive improvement in your life too. See, that description sounds like astigmatism. So, you probably have severe eyestrain basically all the time, and maybe headaches too, especially if you try to read a lot. Glasses should just make all of that go away, after a day or two of weird-feeling adjustment. If you play ball sports, you’ll probably find that your accuracy is bad with glasses on… so just don’t wear them to play if that happens.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How long does it take for light to reach our eyes after reflecting off an object? Is this the reason for the delay in our vision?
Answer: The speed of light in everyday units is approximately a foot per nanosecond. Over ordinary distances, that’s so fast compared to human perception it may as well be instant. No, you have to look at the reality of collecting enough light to get a reasonable exposure, and delays in the human nervous system if you want to understand visual delay. The speed of nerve impulses in the body is about the same as the speed of sound… roughly a foot per millisecond, a full million times slower than light. People can percieve milliseconds, so it’s not beyond belief that the 1/2 millisecond or so it takes for your optic nerve to get a signal to your visual centers (which are right at the back of your head) is actually perceptible. We mostly compensate for these delays without even thinking about it, but careful observation can show them as direct experiences.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What keeps lithium ion batteries from spontaneously discharging once charged? What are the underlying physical mechanisms?
Answer: Nothing, they do spontaneously discharge. They just do it rather slowly. All batteries are specified with a self-discharge rate. For lithium ion, that’s about 3% per month.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If earning a lot of money is my target, what major should I choose? My interest was in computer science, but people are saying to me that don't do it because AI is going to replace it. What should I do?
Answer: AI is not going to replace programmers. It’s just a power tool, and so far a pretty crude one at that. However… don’t go into anything just because of the money. Do something you like doing enough to stick with it, because there is nothing worse than being stuck to a job you hate with golden handcuffs. So… what are you interested in doing enough to do it for 20 years or more? Of the things you like doing that much, what has the best potential return? Understand that if there’s something on that list that you really love, but doesn’t make enough money to live off… there’s your hobby.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for an airplane to land without its nose wheel touching down first? If so, what would happen and would it be due to aerodynamics and physics?
Answer: Correct landing technique for a tricycle airplane is to touch down main gear first, and nose wheel only later. If you don’t, you’re risking a ground loop (basically, in car terms, you spin out and crash). The reason you can do this is that you are flying very slowly, which requires a high angle of attack, which requires a nose-high attitude. This also means that there is a maximum speed at which you can safely touch down, because the angle of attack would be too low and the nose wheel would touch first.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: According to Nvidia CEO Jen-Hsun "Jensen" Huang, coding is dead. Do you agree?
Answer: No. Certainly not yet, because currently AI writes garbage code, and has legal issues that mean most companies should not touch it under any circumstances whatsoever (What’s the license? What was the license on the training data, and does it propagate through the AI? How do you know for sure? What if some of the training data was GPL or AGPL?). Once that is all sorted out, which I’m thinking will take a surprisingly long time, then you get this: people predicted that photography would take artists jobs, and that CNC machining would end the need for skilled machinists, and so forth. But they were wrong: the new tools just make opportunities for people to make more and better stuff. Somewhat different skills may be needed, but the old way persists too. AI is not human-replacement yet, and may never be. But it can be an intellectual power tool, and that’s cool.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to see both the North and South poles from any location on Earth?
Answer: At the same time? No. Though, during a lunar eclipse, it is sometimes possible to see the shadow of both poles at the same time.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can a car be filled with jet-A fuel? Would it cause any damage? If not, what is the reason?
Answer: If it was a diesel car, it would be fine. Just don’t do it a lot without adding a little diesel to each tank. If it were a gasoline car, it’s going to be very unhappy. Probably lots of smoke, maybe some sensor damage, though it might run for a while. Jet-A is not gasoline, it’s very carefully standardised kerosene. Diesel engines run kerosene fine, but it’s not a good enough lubricant for their fuel pumps.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How does an airplane engine use normal gasoline? Can this type of engine be used in cars as well?
Answer: Quick, which of these is the car engine and which is the airplane engine? One of those is from a VW Beetle, the other is a common gasoline engine used in many light airplanes and helicopters, made by Lycoming. As you can see, they’re very, very similar (they would look even more similar if one were upside down). That similarity isn’t accidental or superficial, these really are very close cousins. Airplane engines don’t work well in cars, nor usually vice-versa, because a car engine is not typically expected to run at full throttle for more than a few seconds, whereas an airplane engine might need to do that for hours… but really rapid throttle response is a bad thing in a plane, and a good thing in a car. But those aren’t fundamental differences, they’re adaptation of the basic engine concept to a particular application.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What are the differences between gasoline and jet fuel? Can they be used interchangeably?
Answer: No, they can not be used interchangeably. Jet fuel is high-quality kerosene. You can run it in many diesel engines, if you’re careful about fuel pump lubrication, but a gasoline engine won’t like it at all. You can also use it to run any kerosene-fired heater or other appliance. Aviation gasoline is high-octane leaded gasoline, and will work in any gasoline engine that will tolerate the lead (most road vehicle engines built in the last 40 years will not).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for small single-engine planes to use regular fuel instead of aviation gas (avgas)?
Answer: Some do. You have to use the fuel the engine was built for. You can’t just put car fuel in any old plane and fly it, that will result in severe engine damage. However, some manufacturers, including Rotax, make engines that require car fuel (and will be damaged if you try to run avgas), and some manufacturers (especially Austro Engines) make diesels for aircraft, which will run either road diesel or jet fuel.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can electric guitars be custom-made? If so, what is the average cost?
Answer: Yes, they can be custom made. It’s pretty expensive. You would have to be in the market for a very high-end guitar to start with. Just for example, I looked up the Fender custom shop. Their Stratocasters sell for about eight times what the basic factory models do, about nine thousand dollars. If I were to build a guitar for sale, I’d have to charge about four thousand to make any money at all, so this seems reasonable. My guitars each took about a thousand in parts (and I make my own pickups, which saves a ton of money). I expect professional luthiers have to charge something close to what Fender does.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it a good idea to purchase an old Fender electric guitar and upgrade its parts to meet modern standards?
Answer: It’s an even better idea to restore it; the parts you put on should be equivalent to the originals, and only replace parts that need it. Older Fender and Gibson guitars are worth quite a bit in original or restored condition. Modified, unless they’re played by someone famous, not so much. If you want to go modding… get a new instrument, or get one custom built.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can two operating systems, such as Windows 10 and Linux, be installed on an external hard drive connected to a PC through a USB port? If yes, what is the process for doing so?
Answer: That depends on exactly which operating systems you intend to install. But usually, yes. Start with the Linux documentation for how to do a dual boot setup, and how to install on external drives, because that’s where the boot process and how to get Windows installed will be explained. Expect it to take quite a bit of time and a lot of reading.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: If oil enters the exhaust from the turbo, is the turbo 100% ruined? The reason for oil in exhaust is that diesel contaminated the oil. I had about 5.5 litres of diesel/fuel in the engine, etc.
Answer: It might well be perfectly fine. But you’re going to have to get someone to check that. Cleaning it up and replacing the seals and bearings might be in order anyway.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can an internal combustion engine run on two different types of fuel, such as ethanol and gasoline?
Answer: Sure. Many late model car engines have sensors that allow them to run on arbitrary mixtures of ethanol and gasoline. Many older diesels can run on pretty much any oily liquid that burns. Newer ones add a few more requirements, but still can run on a wide variety of stuff.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What type of fret wire is commonly used on guitars? Is it made of nickel, stainless steel, or another material?
Answer: Nickel alloy is standard. Stainless steel and bronze are options (bronze is seldom used on electric guitars, much more common on acoustic, because electric guitar strings have to have steel cores and that is harder than bronze). There’s a brass alloy specifically developed for frets called EVO Gold. This is ideal if you have a nickel allergy, as it has zero nickel content (stainless still has some nickel, but might also be OK).

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is the best brand or model of cheap, beginner's electric guitar for learning to play heavy metal?

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can vintage microphones still produce high-quality sound when connected to modern equipment, such as a computer microphone input?
Answer: Yes. Microphones have been a mature technology for a very long time. 1930s microphones were already very good. 1960s microphones were about as good as current ones in many respects, so much so that some of those designs are still in production. You do need to be a bit careful, though, because normal computer inputs are intended for one specific kind of modern microphone, and most older microphones will not work correctly. However… a studio audio interface will work fine with most of them.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How does an interpreted language convert source code into machine code without compiling it first?
Answer: A purely interpreted language doesn’t convert source code into machine code at all. It reads source code and directly does what it says. In practice, this means it has tokenised and parsed at least some of the program, then taken the resulting syntax tree and, rather than convert that to machine code or assembler instructions and append them to the compiled program, instead it calls out to implementations directly.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it true that engineers at Google are not allowed to use Google search internally due to security concerns?
