Question: What is the minimum number of lines of code required for a beginner to write a simple program?

Question: How do scientists gather information about the inside of a black hole if it cannot be seen? Do they rely on theories and observations of gravity and space-time?

Question: Is it possible to play in standard tuning on a drop D tuned guitar, and vice versa? Can someone learn both tunings simultaneously?
Answer: It doesn’t work like that. You play the guitar using whatever tuning the guitar is in. What finger goes where to produce a particular sound changes, but the sounds you are going for don’t. What combinations of notes are possible changes, so you may have to use different voicings for some parts. Songs are written for particular tunings, sometimes. And yes, you can learn multiple tunings. After a while, you get good at understanding tunings, and you don’t really need to ‘learn a tuning’ so much as just ‘learn this song, which by the way is in oddball tuning X’. And of course… you can decide to tinker with the arrangement so you don’t need the odd tuning.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can you provide an explanation for why time slows down near objects with strong gravitational fields, like neutron stars or black holes, but not near planets or the Sun which have weaker gravitational fields in comparison?
Answer: Time does slow down near smaller objects too… just much less. So, for example, it shows up in the orbit of Mercury as a tiny change in the shape of the orbit due to gravitational time dilation from the Sun. A dedicated amateur astronomer could do the work to demonstrate that, over a period of a year or two, with reasonably priced equipment. It shows up due to gravitational time dilation from the Earth too, if you have good enough equipment to detect it. That’s within the budget of a (moderately wealthy) amateur scientist. I could do it if I wanted, with my own money. State of the art timing equipment can detect the gravitational time dilation due to the mass of a moderate sized mountain. I could do that too, though I couldn’t pay for it.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Why is a gravitational redshift only visible when looking at distant stars from space, but not on Earth's surface?
Answer: It is detectable on Earth’s surface, you just need extremely high precision equipment to do it. But with a few atomic clocks and some way to take one of them to the top of a mountain for a while and back down, you can demonstrate gravitational redshift on Earth. Moving atomic clocks around is a bit tricky, because they’re quite power-hungry, but it can be arranged, and has been, many times. As General Relativity predicts, an atomic clock runs very slightly fast at the top of a mountain, compared to what it does at sea level. Several everyday technologies, most notably GPS, Starlink, and 5G cellular, have to deal with this in their time calculations or they simply would not work. GPS and Starlink also have to deal with the corrections due to the orbital speed of their satellites.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How do I tell if my violin is legit? It is an Antonius Stradivarius Cremonensis Faciebat Anno 1713 Czechoslovakia.
Answer: It isn’t a Strad, it’s a copy of a 1713 Strad made in Czechoslovakia. However, that doesn’t make it a bad violin, nor does it mean it’s worth nothing. Take it to an expert, it could easily be a professional or soloist grade instrument and worth quite a bit. Or not. The point is, from the given information, nobody can tell.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Gravity isn’t a force but mass (if I’m not mistaken). The stellar objects do attract other objects towards it such as local black-holes, and so do we have our own gravity. Why we do not attract other objects but the stellar objects do?
Answer: Simple: we do have our own gravity and attract other objects, but due to the general weakness of gravity as a force, you can’t tell. Under lab conditions, you can measure the gravity of everyday sized objects, but it’s a fiddly experiment and takes a long time. One of the things you have to be careful of in doing that experiment is where the people in the lab are, because their gravity can mess it up. Best to set it up with automatic recording equipment, leave, and lock the door for a few days.

Question: How do you fix a broken pickup on a bass guitar?

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What company makes an electric bass guitar that has only one bolt holding the neck on? I've tried Googling it (images and all), but every guitar they show with a bolted on neck has four bolts?
Answer: There’s a straightforward structural reason for that. The neck needs to be constrained sufficiently to stay properly positioned, and clamped in to place. Bolt-on necks are primarily there to simplify the joinery of the neck-body interface, to make the instrument both cheaper and more robust. One bolt could be sufficient clamping force to retain a bass neck, but to constrain the neck such that it would not rotate around that bolt would require precision joinery around the neck pocket. That rather defeats the purpose of using a bolt-on at all. Three is the minimum possible to constrain the position and all rotations, but the trouble with that is that you also want the bolts to be quite short, and that limits the clamping force you can generate. So most bolt-ons have at least four bolts, sometimes as many as six.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible for a broken truss rod to cause buzzing on an electric guitar?
Answer: Yes, it is possible. It’s unlikely, though, as the truss rod balances string tension, so the usual result of a broken truss rod is that the action is unplayably high, rather than too low. A truss rod that is jammed too tight might do it. However, there are many possible causes of buzzes, and really you want someone who knows how to properly set up a guitar to take a look and figure out what is really going on. A broken truss rod is a very expensive repair (so expensive it’s probably uneconomic on a cheap guitar, and possibly worth just replacing the whole neck even on a fairly high end instrument), whereas most of the things that cause buzzes can be fixed cheaply. Note: if you go price guitar truss rods, you’ll find they’re a cheap part (about $30). Replacing one is expensive because of the amount of work involved, and the potential for having to replace other parts or repair damage caused by getting the truss rod out as well.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: How do I make my over a 100 year old violin playable? I know barely anything about violins. I know I need a bridge, rosin, and to tune it of course. Should I change the strings? Should I change the hairs on the bow or will the ones I have work?
Answer: You should take it to a violin luthier for a setup. You should also get it valued at the same time so you know how much to insure it for. You will almost certainly need to get the bow hairs changed. The ones you have could be in any condition at all, and there’s no easy way to tell. That’s routine maintenance, and not very expensive. You also should get new strings. They don’t last forever, are not expensive, and again the condition is unknown. Your luthier can supply some, and you can’t put them on until after the rest of the work is done anyway. If you don’t have a bridge, you probably don’t have a soundpost either, and there are other items (particularly the tailwire) that should be looked at. Bridges and soundposts are custom fit to the instrument; what you buy is a blank that needs further work to install. These are not things you want to be practicing making with a possibly valuable old instrument. It’s likely the tuning pegs won’t hold; a luthier can fix this easily, but it takes a long while to explain how to figure out which of the five or six tricks you should use, and using the wrong one makes it worse. Possibly it might need new ones. You haven’t mentioned it, but if the bridge is missing, the tailpiece might be too. That can be replaced also.

Question: Why are there so many people using Apple? There are so many cheap and better options.
Answer: There are cheap options. They’re not dependable. There are better options. They’re typically more expensive, often much more expensive. There are also options for situations Apple doesn’t cover. They’re sometimes spectacularly expensive. If you need pro gear, you pay for pro gear… and Apple is actually inexpensive as pro gear goes. For example, compare a MacBook Pro with an Lenovo X1 Carbon of similar specs. You’ll find that the X1 is a little more expensive, its maintenance contract is significantly more expensive, but the X1 is a tad lighter, and of course will run Linux or Windows natively, which might make it a better option for your workload. Or compare a Panasonic Toughbook. Low specs, but can be expected to survive till it is obsolete being used daily on a construction site or down a mine (you can even pressure wash it). Very expensive, but cheaper than replacing ten X1s or MacBook Pros. A plastic chassis consumer laptop will not survive a year with a “road warrior” or a week on a construction site. A MacBook Pro or X1 should survive a road warrior, most years. A Toughbook definitely will, but said road warrior will be cursing the weight, and they don’t really need quite that much durability… but construction site and mine workers definitely do.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What are the chances that someone at Google steals my novel if I put it on Google Drive?
Answer: Zero. Less than zero. Your novel is worth approximately nothing, and in any case is inherently copyright. So, if someone did steal it, they’d make about nothing, and in the unlikely event they did make some money, they’d face a lawsuit that would wipe it all out. In comparison, anyone at Google who is even in a position to recognise that you have a novel on Google Drive is already about to be fired… and their job is worth much more than your novel is right now. So everybody there will be working quite hard to avoid knowing you have a novel in Drive (it’s fine if you told them so, but they won’t get to it by technical means). You are far more likely to find that if your novel gets stolen, it was by someone at a publisher that you submitted it to. And even the chance of that is about zero, though it has happened a few times. You are also far more likely to have your novel stolen right off your own computer, and that’s super unlilkely too, just because there’s no money in it.

Question: Will playing the violin with a missing sound post crack the face of the instrument?

Question: Is it possible to use aluminum instead of wood for making guitars and other stringed instruments? Would it be a suitable material for the body parts such as the neck and bridge?
Answer: Yes, it’s possible. For some parts, like electric guitar bridges, it’s completely normal to use aluminium. Others, like tuners, it’s not quite normal but still common. Aluminium is also a common ingredient in a bronze alloy used for some acoustic guitar strings. People have used aluminium for necks, fretboards, and even pretty much the whole instrument. It’s not actually a great material for neck and fretboard, because while it sounds fine and looks cool, it also feels too cold to play comfortably. I played an aluminium neck bass once, it sounded great but gave me cramp very quickly because the room was pretty cold. Double bass players will be familiar with this issue because the strings themselves are enough of a heat sink to be a problem. Aluminium frets are a bad idea, it’s too soft and will wear out quickly. Composites like carbon fiber and Richlite are usually preferable if you’re looking for non-wood alternatives for structural parts. Plastics are possible, 3D printed guitar bodies are quite doable. Nevertheless… this is a real instrument: Note the wood neck.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can guitar pickups be replaced with different types, such as switching from single-coil to dual-coil or vice versa? How challenging is this process and what tools or skills are required?
Answer: It can be anything from almost trivial (if the pickups you want are available in the same case and mounting format as the ones you have) to so impossible it would be cheaper and easier to just buy a guitar that already had the pickups you want. If your instrument has humbuckers (dual coil), it may be a wiring change only to give you a switch that turns them into single coils; all the guitars I have built have that switch (a pull switch on the volume knob) because it’s so easy. If you have single coils and want humbuckers… that’s not easy. If you have something that isn’t either a trad single coil or a trad humbucker… you probably have few options but to replace like with like. In all these cases… it’s not easy to describe how to DIY it, because there are way too many options. Five main pickup formats, each of which have hundreds or thousands of different pickups available, many of which can be wired in multiple different ways. Wiring mods can make any pickup sound very different; just changing the tone pot and capacitor can make a massive difference, let alone anything more complex. And of course… it’s possible to custom-build pickups, if you still can’t find what you want. It might even be easier, because a good pickup builder can take a description of what you want and make it happen, and it may well be price-competitive too. So… take thee to a good luthier, and ask them about it. But be specific: you have a particular guitar, and you want to achieve something different that it doesn’t do right now.

Question: Is it possible to connect an electric bass directly to a speaker without using an amplifier?

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can two acoustic guitars with different tunings still play together without sounding out of tune or bad?
Answer: Any instruments with different tunings can play together. This is one of the points of music theory, actually. Learning how to do that. Say you take a guitar tuned in E standard, and another in ’D standard’, in other words all the strings tuned a tone lower. Now play a G chord on the guitar tuned in E, and play the shape that would be an A chord in E standard on the guitar tuned in D. The A shape sounds as a G chord, which of course sounds just fine with the G chord on the other guitar. Do something similar with the whole arrangement, and a song will work just fine. A symphony orchestra has string instruments with four different tunings, as well as at least five different other tunings across the wind instruments, and yet it works. Very often an orchestra’s bass section will be using several different tunings too, just in the one section (while I was playing, it was pretty common to have the principal playing a 5 string, me playing drop-D, and everyone else in standard tuning).

Question: Why do some mirrorless cameras still have a pentaprism shape in front of the electronic viewfinder?

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can using heavier or lighter strings on an electric guitar affect its tuning? If so, to what extent? Is there a way to prevent this from happening?
Answer: Yes, it will. Well, not tuning, but intonation. The difference is this: tuning is the pitches to which you adjust the open strings. That you can get correct easily with any reasonable string. But intonation is the pitch at each fret. Even if the open string is in tune, that does not mean all the frets are. When the instrument was set up, it was intonated to a particular set of strings. If you change them to another set of the exact same type, there should be minimal effect on the intonation. If, however, you change gauges, or change to a material with a different density, then the change in tension as you fret notes will be different, and the intonation will be off. In other words, the open strings can be right, but the further up the fretboard you go, the worse the tuning gets. This can be fixed by redoing the intonation parts of the setup… adjusting the bridge saddle positions, heights, and maybe the truss rod, so that the pitches line up with the frets again. If you have a tremelo, that will need adjusted too (which takes a lot of work… this isn’t easy and won’t be cheap). Either learn how to do this properly, which is way too much to describe in a Quora answer, or decide on what strings you want to use, then take the instrument to a setup technician or luthier and get them to get it right… then keep using exactly the same kind of strings.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is flying actually as safe as we perceive it to be, considering the number of planes in service at any given time?
Answer: It’s actually much safer than you probably think. Flying is by far the safest way to travel long distances. Rail is a close second. Even flying light aircraft, which are much less safe than the airlines, you’re more likely to have a road accident getting to the airport than you are during a flight. It doesn’t even matter much how close to the airport you live, either, unless you’re right next door.

Question: Are all airplanes equipped with a glass cockpit or are there still some older models with analogue instruments in the cockpit?
Answer: Analogue instruments are basically obsolete on new aircraft, because the digital versions are now cheaper. Though, analogue instruments are still available as options on some types. However, there are lots of old aircraft still flying with original instrumentation, and the parts and equipment to maintain them are still available.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What maximum wind speed is acceptable for cross wind landing?
Answer: It depends on the airplane, and the answer may be in the manual. At the very least there will be a “maximum demonstrated crosswind”, which shows that during the certification testing someone landed it in those conditions. It’s not necessarily the actual limiting crosswind, it’s just the maximum they could find. I have personally doubled the demonstrated maximum (in a Piper Archer), so good technique helps a lot… but you really better know the airplane well before trying that. Or, there could be a complex set of criteria to allow you to calculate the maximum crosswind, based on aircraft weight and air density and whatnot. If you’re lucky, there will also be software available to do that calculation.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Do I need to purchase my flight tickets to and from New Zealand before applying for a visitors visa (from South Africa)?
Answer: No. In fact, you should apply for the visa first, that way you don’t have to risk change fees in case it takes longer than expected.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Is it possible to build an aircraft with only one wing and make the center or pressure dynamically match the center of gravity by quickly moving fore and aft some kind of mass?
Answer: Yes: One wing, no control surfaces of any kind, pilot moves their own mass around to control it. There are some clever things going on with flexure in the wing to make a hang glider more controllable, but they’re there to make them nicer to fly, it would work with a completely rigid wing.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: Can you take off without flaps on an airplane? If so, how long will it fly before it crashes due to lack of lift?
Answer: In small planes, if you have a long enough runway, you can safely take off, fly around, and land again without a problem. You do have to take off much faster than you would with the flaps, which is why you need more runway. Really big aircraft, including many airliners and military transports, don’t have tyres which would survive going that fast on the ground, nor would their landing gear stay intact at that speed. But in principle, if runways were long enough and airplane wheels strong enough, no particular problem. Trying to take off at a speed calculated for a certain amount of flap extension without those flaps actually extended, though, is a really serious mistake, and will probably lead to a crash one way or another.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What is it like to fly as a passenger in an Airbus A380, the largest passenger plane in the world? What do you see and feel when flying at night or day time?
Answer: Not a lot different from any other large airplane. The A380 is relatively quiet as airliners go, inherently has slightly more space per passenger, and has a slightly lower cabin altitude than most earlier aircraft, so you arrive feeling a little less worn down by the travel. But the two later aircraft you commonly travel in, the A350 and 787 Dreamliner, also have those characteristics. So it’s more a generational step in airliner design, rather than anything specific to the A380. The A380 is also so big you have less chance of getting a window seat, and anyway the view is no different from any other airliner.

Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: What do pilots see outside through the windows of planes at night that makes them turn off their lights for a while before landing?
Answer: The runway they’re intending to land on, or at least the guide lights for it. That’s the most important thing. But also other air traffic and the warning lights on tall buildings and towers. Most of the time if it is at all possible, pilots fly the last stages of landing approaches visually and by hand. It’s much less work than doing a high category instrument approach, and autoland is the hardest by far. Visual approaches also let the airports fit in more traffic, so the schedules are often made assuming most of the time aircraft will be using them. It’s much easier to see out of a window if the lights inside are dim; they’re not usually all the way off, as you do still have to be able to see inside the plane as well.

Question: Can you feel when a plane is rotating due to its velocity relative to the ground changing as it flies along?
Answer: Kind of, but it’s not at all reliable… if you try to estimate what a plane is doing with your eyes shut, or with no visibility outside, you will certainly be wrong after a few seconds, and drastically, dangerously wrong after a minute or so. If you turn your head quickly while a plane is turning, it gets even worse. That’s why flying on instruments is a fairly long course… not only is it complicated, but you also have to learn never to trust what your body is telling you, and instead rely on the instruments only. Which means of course that you have to have several instruments for each component of the plane’s behaviour and cross-check them, because one might fail, and you can’t trust your intuition at all. This is also one reason many people get airsick… their body’s balance organs are telling them the plane is turning or rolling when it isn’t, but their eyes and the seat of their pants are telling them they’re upright, and the inconsistency tricks the brain into thinking they’ve been poisoned.

Question: How does tipping work in Australia? Is it customary to leave a tip after every meal at restaurants, or does it vary depending on the type of restaurant?
Answer: It is never usual nor expected to tip. Service staff are paid decently, and don’t need tips to earn a living. Most times when paying with a card, the staff will skip right over the tip screen, if their machine even has one (most Australian bank card machines have that screen disabled by default). If paying in cash, there’s ordinarily a jar where you might leave coins, but again… not expected. If someone does something truly exceptional and worth acknowledging, then leave a tip.

Question: Can I acquire a native-like proficiency in a foreign language? If not, can I at least reduce my foreign accent to a level that nobody would be able to guess where I grew up? I am very ashamed of my place of origin and don't want anyone to know it.
Answer: You can probably adjust your accent to something that won’t place you, that’s entirely possible. My wife, for example, has a light Australian accent in English, an English accent in Romanian, a strong Romanian accent in French and Spanish, but a French accent in German. Yet she was born in none of those countries (though the Aussie accent is real, that’s where she went to school). My own accent is clearly from either Australia or New Zealand, but these days people have a hard time telling which. It’s a lot of work to consciously change an accent though. Accent coaches exist, so getting professional help may be possible. Maybe you should work on the shame instead, that will keep eating you from the inside anyway. Look at it like this: none of us choose our place of origin or our parents, so we can’t fairly be blamed for them either. It’s what we do with those circumstances that defines us. That means that if someone judges you for your origin, race, or ancestors… they’re being unfair, and you should be annoyed, not ashamed.

Question: Is there a difference in sound between a stacked double coil and a regular double coil guitar pickup?
Answer: Absolutely there is. Aside from the output level difference, which can be compensated for, there’s a very big difference in what parts of the string are being sensed, and in the shape of the field around the string. Every little detail of the shape of that field translates into some part of the character of the sound. Since these two have completely different field shapes, they’re inevitably going to have totally different sounds. Stacked coils sound like single coils, mostly. Which is the point of them. Both a stacked humbucker and a single coil have one “window” on the string. A humbucker sounds very different, due to having two separate sensing “windows” on the string; the two coils therefore see somewhat different harmonic structure, which leads to some harmonics being enhanced and some reduced. Also, the parts of the string that are in the sensing window of the pickup (even pickups you are not using) get “braked” a bit by the magnetic field. Humbuckers have a stronger field, so the string is damped somewhat more.

Question: What is the best single-engine two-seater trainer plane for a beginner pilot? Is it worth spending more money on a better plane or less on one that's cheaper but still effective?
Answer: Don’t even think about buying a plane as a beginner pilot. Until you have your PPL, at least, you should just rent planes. Even after that unless you’re going to be doing more than a couple of hundred hours a year. It will save you a huge amount of money, and you won’t be risking buying something you won’t want later. It also lets you rent the particular type you need for whatever the mission of the day is. Later in your training that will get really important… one day you need a twin, another you can do the job in a single, but you need aerobatic capability. On top of that, owning an airplane is a lot of work, arranging for its maintenance and paperwork to stay certified. That gets more expensive the less you fly it, too. Renting outsources all of that to professionals who have a fleet to deal with, so they can do it way more efficiently than you could. Getting my PPL I flew four different types, and a fairly large fraction of the school’s fleet.

Question: How difficult is it to write classical music on your computer using VSTs (virtual instruments) if you cannot play any real instruments yourself?

Question: How can I repair or replace cracked/loose frets on an acoustic/electric guitar's neck?
Answer: Fretwork is a really hard skill to learn, and the tools are expensive. Now… if you want to spend a full time month or two learning how, and can afford to spend about as much as a good guitar on tools, and are willing to damage a few guitar fretboards in the process, go learn. Your first three or four fret jobs will not be very good… and relacements are harder than making new instruments. If, however, you just want your guitar playable… find a guitar repair shop or guitar luthier, and get them to do the job for you. It won’t cost all that much, so if it’s a decent instrument it’s worth doing. It’s relatively cheap to get done because it doesn’t take all that long for an expert, the tools last a really long time, and the materials are not expensive.

Question: I need a bass guitar for recording. I normally play guitar not bass. Can you recommend a useful, versatile bass, electric or electric/acoustic?

Question: Are there any airplanes that still use manual flying? If so, why would you need the option of manual flying if there's already an auto-pilot system available?
Answer: Almost all airplanes that carry people have to use manual flight controls for part of every flight. Those that can do a complete flight fully automatically, including takeoff, almost never actually do that. You’re thinking of a plane’s auto-pilot like Tesla full-self-driving. It’s not that. It’s cruise control, more or less. Not all that many commercial airliners even have auto-land, and automatic takeoff is so rare you may as well ignore it as a possibility. Auto-land is only used when either it’s the only way to get on the ground at the destination, or if the crew needs to do one to stay certified to do them. That’s because it’s way, way, way more work for the crew to set up and do an auto-land than it is to just hand-fly the plane. Auto-taxi on the ground exists, but again, it’s only used when it has to be. Many operators prefer to ignore it and arrange to get the plane towed on the occasions when it is necessary. So a typical airline flight has maybe ten minutes of hand flying, but that’s takeoff and a few minutes of the departure and the last few minutes of the landing approach, plus however long it takes to taxi. Small planes often don’t even have an autopilot, and when they do it’s typically more fun and less work to hand fly, unless you’re in bad weather and busy with instrument navigation.

Question: Can an Australian permanently move to New Zealand without any problems, as long as they have citizenship there? What would happen if you didn't have a job already lined up when you arrived in New Zealand?
Answer: You don’t even need citizenship… Australians are automatically permanent residents in NZ. Name: Andrew McGregor
Question: I am 17 years old, I’ve been super into space but I have a question. If we could figure out how to recreate nuclear fusion like in stars on a small scale or manipulate atomic density, could we potentially manipulate gravity?
Answer: We don’t know. At the moment it looks like gravity manipulation is probably impossible, but since we don’t have a good theory for why there is gravity, there’s a limit to how sure we can be about that. However, the theories we do have that describe what gravity does certainly don’t give us any kind of practical handle on how to go about modifying gravity. So that one needs some presently unknown science, and there is no way at all to know how long it might take to answer definitively or what the answer will be. Fusion we can do, and will do eventually, once someone decides to get out of NASA style development and do a SpaceX on it. But it’s not relevant to gravity manipulation, except in so far as gravity manipulation might well need a ton of power. “Manipulating atomic density” is technobabble… there’s nothing in actual physics that would make that set of words mean anything useful. Cute in Star Trek or a Marvel movie, but not real world science.
